\section{Distinguishability and separation}

Three questions should not be conflated:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Formulas $\mathcal L_1,\mathcal L_2$ are semantically different when
      $\varsigma(\mathcal L_1)\neq\varsigma(\mathcal L_2)$.
\item Valuations $v,w$ are observationally distinguishable by $\Phi$ when
      $o_\Phi(v)\neq o_\Phi(w)$.
\item Points are topologically separated according to the neighborhoods
      available in $\tau_\Phi$.
\end{enumerate}
Overlap between two truth regions does not by itself establish topological
indistinguishability.

\begin{proposition}[Semantic XOR criterion]
For formulas $\mathcal L_1,\mathcal L_2$,
\[
 \varsigma(\mathcal L_1)\neq\varsigma(\mathcal L_2)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \varsigma(\mathcal L_1\Updownarrow\mathcal L_2)\neq\varnothing.
\]
At a particular valuation $v$, their truth values are distinct exactly when
$v\in\varsigma(\mathcal L_1\Updownarrow\mathcal L_2)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The XOR truth region is the symmetric difference
\[
 \varsigma(\mathcal L_1)\mathbin{\triangle}
 \varsigma(\mathcal L_2).
\]
It is nonempty exactly when the two truth regions are unequal.
\end{proof}

Observing only $\mathcal L_1\wedge\mathcal L_2$ gives one positive bit and
groups together all three ways in which the conjunction can be false.  Replacing
that observation by the pair $\Phi=(\mathcal L_1,\mathcal L_2)$ refines those
states according to the realized truth vectors $(1,1),(1,0),(0,1),(0,0)$.
Adding both negations makes the nonempty truth-pattern cells clopen.  This is
the precise observational sense in which the conjuncts become distinguishable.

\begin{definition}[Topological indistinguishability]
Points $v,w\in\Omega_P$ are topologically indistinguishable when they belong to
exactly the same open sets of $\tau_\Phi$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Indistinguishability theorem]
For $v,w\in\Omega_P$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $v$ and $w$ are topologically indistinguishable in $\tau_\Phi$;
\item $v$ and $w$ have the same subbasic open memberships;
\item $o_\Phi(v)=o_\Phi(w)$;
\item $v\sim_\Phi w$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Equality of all open memberships implies equality of subbasic memberships.
Subbasic memberships are exactly the coordinates of $o_\Phi$.  Conversely,
equality of signatures gives equality of membership in every finite
intersection of subbasic opens and hence in every union of such intersections.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[$T_0$ quotient]
The space $(\Omega_P,\tau_\Phi)$ is $T_0$ exactly when $o_\Phi$ is injective.  Its
Kolmogorov quotient is naturally identified with the set $o_\Phi(\Omega_P)$ of
realized signatures, equipped with the subspace upper-set topology inherited
from $\mathbb S^I$.
\end{corollary}

The next separation level requires distinguishability in both directions.

\begin{proposition}[$T_1$ and complete finite separation]
The observation space is $T_1$ exactly when, for every distinct $v,w$,
\[
  o_\Phi(v)\nsubseteq o_\Phi(w)
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  o_\Phi(w)\nsubseteq o_\Phi(v).
\]
Equivalently, $o_\Phi$ is injective and its image is an antichain.  A
finite $T_1$ space is discrete; therefore finite Hausdorff observation spaces
are discrete as well.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
There is an open containing $v$ but not $w$ exactly when some observation is
true at $v$ and false at $w$, which is equivalent to
$o_\Phi(v)\nsubseteq o_\Phi(w)$.  The $T_1$ condition requires this in both
directions.  In a finite $T_1$ space, each singleton is the finite intersection
of open complements of the other singletons, so every singleton is open.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Sierpi\'nski observation space]
Let $P=\{X\}$ and $\Phi=(X)$.  With valuations $0,1$, the topology is
\[
  \tau_\Phi=\{\varnothing,\{1\},\{0,1\}\}.
\]
It is $T_0$ but not $T_1$.  The positive observation $X$ distinguishes $1$
from $0$, but no positive observation in $\Phi$ distinguishes $0$ from $1$.
This is the canonical two-point example of asymmetric observation.
\end{example}

\section{Asymmetric separation and the specialization preorder}

We use the specialization convention
\[
 v\preceq_\Phi w
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \text{every open neighborhood of $v$ contains $w$}.
\]
Some authors use the reverse convention; the direction is fixed here by the
display above.

Because $\Omega_P$ is finite, every point has a smallest open neighborhood
\[
 N_\Phi(v):=\bigcap\{U\in\tau_\Phi:v\in U\}.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Positive-information order]
For all $v,w\in\Omega_P$,
\[
 v\preceq_\Phi w
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 o_\Phi(v)\subseteq o_\Phi(w).
\]
Moreover,
\[
 N_\Phi(v)
 =\bigcap_{i\in o_\Phi(v)}\varsigma(\varphi_i)
 =\{w:o_\Phi(v)\subseteq o_\Phi(w)\}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If every open containing $v$ contains $w$, this holds for every subbasic open,
so every observation true at $v$ is true at $w$.  Conversely, if
$o_\Phi(v)\subseteq o_\Phi(w)$, then every basic open containing $v$ contains $w$,
and therefore every open containing $v$ contains $w$.  The neighborhood formula
follows.
\end{proof}

Thus $w$ preserves all positive information observable at $v$ and may satisfy
additional observations.  Failure of symmetry is not a defect: it records that
positive evidence can separate one direction without separating the reverse.
After quotienting by $\sim_\Phi$, the preorder becomes the inclusion order on
realized signatures.

\section{Distances on observation signatures}

Coordinatewise XOR naturally produces a difference vector.  Let
$\mathbf a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be positive real weights.  As noted in Section~3,
these formulas use complete semantic profiles, even when the topology is read as
an interface for affirmative certificates.  The distances are deliberately
presentation-dependent: changing weights, duplicating coordinates, or replacing
$\Phi$ by a different family that generates the same topology can change their
numerical values.

\begin{definition}[Observable XOR difference]
Define
\[
 \Delta_\Phi(v,w)
 :=o_\Phi(v)\Updownarrow o_\Phi(w)
 :=\bigl(b_i(v)\Updownarrow b_i(w)\bigr)_{i\in I}.
\]
This vector identifies exactly which observations disagree.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Symmetric signature distance]
Define the weighted Hamming distance between signatures by
\[
 d_\Phi(v,w)
 :=\sum_{i\in I} a_i\lvert b_i(v)-b_i(w)\rvert.
\]
This is a standard weighted form of Hamming distance \cite{Hamming1950}.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
The function $d_\Phi$ is a pseudometric on $\Omega_P$, and
\[
 d_\Phi(v,w)=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 v\sim_\Phi w.
\]
Consequently, $d_\Phi$ induces a metric on the underlying set
$\Omega_P/{\sim_\Phi}$.  If $\tau_{d_\Phi}$ denotes the pseudometric topology on
$\Omega_P$, then
\[
 \tau_{d_\Phi}=\tau_{\Phi^{\pm}}.
\]
The induced metric topology on the finite quotient set is discrete and need not
equal its Kolmogorov quotient topology.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Each coordinate contributes the weighted discrete metric on $\{0,1\}$; their
sum is a pseudometric.  It vanishes exactly when every observation coordinate
agrees.  If $I\neq\varnothing$, every sufficiently small ball at $v$ is exactly the signature
fiber $[v]_\Phi$, while every ball is a union of such fibers.  Hence the
pseudometric topology is the partition topology of Proposition
\ref{prop:two-sided-observation}.  For $I=\varnothing$ there is one fiber and both
topologies are indiscrete.  A genuine metric on a finite set has discrete
topology, giving the final qualification.
\end{proof}

For example, the Sierpi\'nski space of Example 4.6 is already $T_0$, so its
Kolmogorov quotient has the same nondiscrete topology.  Its Hamming metric is
the ordinary discrete two-point metric.  Thus ``metric on the quotient set''
does not mean ``metric inducing the quotient topology.''

Symmetric distance measures disagreement but cannot by itself encode the
direction of the specialization preorder.  For that purpose define the cost of
losing observations.

\begin{definition}[Directed loss distance]
Define
\[
 d_\Phi^+(v,w)
 :=\sum_{i\in I} a_i\,
   \ind[b_i(v)=1\text{ and }b_i(w)=0].
\]
Equivalently, this is weighted set difference from the support of $v$ to the
support of $w$.  In XOR notation the direction is supplied by the source mask:
\[
 d_\Phi^+(v,w)=\sum_{i\in I} a_i b_i(v)
   \bigl(b_i(v)\Updownarrow b_i(w)\bigr).
\]
This finite weighted sum is an elementary directed set-difference construction.
Pavlovic uses the cardinality $\lvert y\setminus x\rvert$, with the opposite
argument orientation from our loss convention \cite[Sec.~2]{Pavlovic2012},
while de Brecht uses a supremum of decaying weights on a countable powerset
\cite[Sec.~4]{deBrecht2013}.
\end{definition}

The theorem below is therefore an explicit coordinate representation for the
chosen observation presentation, not a claim that quasi-metrizability of finite
Alexandrov spaces is new.  In particular, Dovgoshey and Shanin prove that every
$T_0$ Alexandrov space is quasi-metrizable by an equidistant quasi-metric
\cite{DovgosheyShanin2026}.  Here $d_\Phi^+$ works already before the $T_0$
quotient, at the price of being a quasi-\emph{pseudo}metric when distinct points
have the same signature.

\begin{theorem}[Quasi-pseudometric representation]
The function $d_\Phi^+$ is a quasi-pseudometric: it is nonnegative,
$d_\Phi^+(v,v)=0$, and
\[
 d_\Phi^+(v,u)\leq d_\Phi^+(v,w)+d_\Phi^+(w,u).
\]
It also satisfies
\[
 d_\Phi^+(v,w)=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 v\preceq_\Phi w,
\]
and
\[
 d_\Phi(v,w)=d_\Phi^+(v,w)+d_\Phi^+(w,v).
\]
The topology generated by the forward balls, for $r>0$,
\[
 B^+(v,r):=\{w:d_\Phi^+(v,w)<r\}
\]
is exactly $\tau_\Phi$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For each coordinate, an observation lost from $v$ to $u$ must be lost either
from $v$ to $w$ or from $w$ to $u$.  Summing the resulting coordinatewise
inequality proves the triangle inequality.  Vanishing means that no observation
true at $v$ is false at $w$, which is exactly
$o_\Phi(v)\subseteq o_\Phi(w)$.  The symmetrization identity follows because every
disagreement is a loss in exactly one direction.

Every forward ball is upward closed in $\preceq_\Phi$: if $w$ belongs to the ball
and $w\preceq_\Phi u$, then $u$ loses no more observations from $v$ than $w$
does.  Hence every forward ball is $\tau_\Phi$-open.  If $I\neq\varnothing$ and
$0<r\leq\min_{i\in I} a_i$, then
\[
 B^+(v,r)=N_\Phi(v).
\]
The smallest neighborhoods generate $\tau_\Phi$, so the forward-ball topology is
exactly $\tau_\Phi$.  If $I=\varnothing$, the directed distance is identically zero and
every positive-radius forward ball is $\Omega_P$, again giving the correct
indiscrete topology.
\end{proof}

The zero-distance relation of $d_\Phi^+$ recovers the preorder and its forward
balls recover the topology.  Its positive numerical values contain additional
presentation data: changing weights, or adding a topologically redundant
coordinate, can change distances without changing $\preceq_\Phi$ or
$\tau_\Phi$.  This is compatible with the general role of nonsymmetric distance
in generalized metric theory \cite{Lawvere1973}.

\section{Interior, closure, and observational boundary}

Topological operators describe what can be verified or ruled out using the
chosen observations.

\begin{definition}
For an event $E\subseteq\Omega_P$, let
\[
 \Int_\Phi(E):=\Int_{\tau_\Phi}(E),\qquad
 \Cl_\Phi(E):=\Cl_{\tau_\Phi}(E),\qquad
 \bd_\Phi E:=\Cl_\Phi(E)\setminus\Int_\Phi(E).
\]
\end{definition}

The interior $\Int_\Phi(E)$ is the largest observable open event contained in
$E$.  If the actual valuation lies in this interior, a finite conjunction of
available positive observations certifies membership in $E$.  The closure $\Cl_\Phi(E)$ consists of
valuations at which the available observations cannot exclude contact with
$E$.  The boundary $\bd_\Phi E$ is therefore an observational ambiguity region.
Equivalently,
\[
 \bd_\Phi E
 =\Cl_\Phi(E)\cap\Cl_\Phi(\Omega_P\setminus E).
\]
It contains precisely those points whose available neighborhoods cannot settle
membership in $E$ one way or the other.

\begin{proposition}[Finite neighborhood formulas]
For every $E\subseteq\Omega_P$,
\begin{align*}
 \Int_\Phi(E)&=\{v:N_\Phi(v)\subseteq E\},\\
 \Cl_\Phi(E)&=\{v:N_\Phi(v)\cap E\neq\varnothing\}.
\end{align*}
Consequently,
\[
 v\in\bd_\Phi E
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 N_\Phi(v)\cap E\neq\varnothing
 \text{ and }
 N_\Phi(v)\cap(\Omega_P\setminus E)\neq\varnothing.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The point $v$ is interior to $E$ exactly when it has an open neighborhood
contained in $E$.  Since $N_\Phi(v)$ is its smallest neighborhood, this is
equivalent to $N_\Phi(v)\subseteq E$.  A point belongs to the closure of $E$
exactly when each of its neighborhoods meets $E$, which in a finite space is
equivalent to $N_\Phi(v)\cap E\neq\varnothing$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Boundary versus XOR]
The symbol $\bd_\Phi$ denotes the topological boundary operator above.  It is
not the Boolean symmetric-difference operation that removes the overlap of two
formulas.  That Boolean operation is the exclusive remainder
\[
 \varsigma(\mathcal L_1\vee\mathcal L_2)
 \setminus\varsigma(\mathcal L_1\wedge\mathcal L_2)
 =\varsigma(\mathcal L_1\Updownarrow\mathcal L_2).
\]
The two constructions can differ even in the simplest cases: in a discrete
topology every topological boundary is empty, while an XOR truth region
may be nonempty.
\end{remark}

\begin{example}[Boundary of implication under positive observations]
For $\Phi=(X,Y)$,
\[
 E=\varsigma(X\Rightarrow Y)=\{B,C,D\}.
\]
Using the topology in Example 3.6,
\[
 \Int_\Phi(E)=\{B,C\},\qquad
 \Cl_\Phi(E)=\Omega_{X,Y},\qquad
 \bd_\Phi E=\{A,D\}.
\]
Thus $X\Rightarrow Y$ is neither open nor closed in this observation topology.
The point $D$ satisfies the implication but is not positively certifiable as
such using only $X$ and $Y$, while $A$ lies observationally adjacent to
satisfying states despite falsifying the implication.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[XOR region under coarse and discrete observation]
Retain the partition labels $A=X\wedge\neg Y$,
$B=X\wedge Y$, $C=\neg X\wedge Y$, and
$D=\neg X\wedge\neg Y$.  The exclusive truth region is
\[
 E_\oplus:=\varsigma(X\Updownarrow Y)=\{A,C\}.
\]
First use only the positive observations $\Phi=(X,Y)$.  The smallest
neighborhoods are
\[
 N_\Phi(A)=\{A,B\},\quad N_\Phi(B)=\{B\},\quad
 N_\Phi(C)=\{B,C\},\quad N_\Phi(D)=\Omega_{X,Y}.
\]
Hence no nonempty $\tau_\Phi$-open set is contained in $E_\oplus$, while the
neighborhoods of $A$, $C$, and $D$ each meet it.  Thus
\[
 \Int_\Phi(E_\oplus)=\varnothing,\qquad
 \Cl_\Phi(E_\oplus)=\{A,C,D\},\qquad
 \bd_\Phi E_\oplus=\{A,C,D\}.
\]
The points $A$ and $C$ belong to the XOR region but are not positively
certifiable using only $X$ and $Y$, because their smallest neighborhoods also
contain $B$.  The point $D$ is not in the XOR region, but it remains on its
boundary because every positive-observation neighborhood of $D$ contains both
XOR and non-XOR valuations.

Now take the two-sided observation family
\[
 \Phi^{\pm}=(X,\neg X,Y,\neg Y).
\]
Its topology is discrete.  Therefore $E_\oplus$ is both open and closed, and
\[
 \Int_{\Phi^{\pm}}(E_\oplus)
 =\Cl_{\Phi^{\pm}}(E_\oplus)
 =\{A,C\},
 \qquad
 \bd_{\Phi^{\pm}}E_\oplus=\varnothing.
\]
The XOR truth set is unchanged by the topology; only its observable boundary
changes.  This is the distinction between Boolean symmetric difference and topological
ambiguity.  Figure~\ref{fig:xor-four-cell} displays the same calculation on
the four truth-pattern cells.
\end{example}

\subsection{Open truth regions and Heyting implication}

The opens of any topology form a Heyting algebra.  For
$U,V\in\tau_\Phi$, define
\[
 U\Rightarrow_H V
 :=\Int_\Phi\bigl((\Omega_P\setminus U)\cup V\bigr),
 \qquad
 \neg_H U:=\Int_\Phi(\Omega_P\setminus U).
\]
Then
\[
 U\cap(U\Rightarrow_H V)\subseteq V
\]
is topological Modus Ponens, and
\[
 (U\Rightarrow_H V)\cap\neg_H V\subseteq\neg_H U
\]
is topological Modus Tollens.  In a discrete topology the interiors do nothing,
and these reduce to their classical truth-set forms.  In a nondiscrete
observation topology, the interior records the loss imposed by requiring the
result to remain observable.

Indeed, for every open $W$,
\[
 W\subseteq U\Rightarrow_H V
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 W\cap U\subseteq V,
\]
which is the defining Heyting adjunction.  The two displayed inference
inequalities follow from it.  These open-set operations belong to standard
topological semantics \cite{McKinseyTarski1944,Vickers2007}; they should be
distinguished from the classical truth-region operations used earlier.  A full intuitionistic
interpretation would assign open sets to atoms and evaluate compound formulas
recursively in this Heyting algebra.

For example, in the Sierpi\'nski space of Example~4.6, interpret $X$ by the
open $\{1\}$.  Then $\neg_H\{1\}=\varnothing$ and
$\neg_H\neg_H\{1\}=\Omega_X$, whereas the interior of the classical truth
region $\varsigma(\neg\neg X)=\{1\}$ is still $\{1\}$.  Recursive Heyting
evaluation therefore differs from taking one final interior of a classical
truth region.

\section{Information refinement and logical update}

The phrase ``acquiring information'' can describe two mathematically different
operations.

\subsection{Refining the observations}

Let $\Phi=(\varphi_i)_{i\in I}$ and $\Psi=(\psi_j)_{j\in J}$, where
$I\subseteq J$ and $\psi_i=\varphi_i$ for every $i\in I$.  Thus $\Psi$ extends
$\Phi$ while retaining the identities of its old coordinates.

\begin{theorem}[Refinement theorem]
For such an indexed extension $\Phi\hookrightarrow\Psi$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $\tau_\Phi\subseteq\tau_\Psi$;
\item $v\sim_\Psi w$ implies $v\sim_\Phi w$;
\item $\preceq_\Psi\,\subseteq\,\preceq_\Phi$ as relations;
\item if $\Psi$ retains the weights $a_i$ on $i\in I$, then
      $d_\Psi^+(v,w)\geq d_\Phi^+(v,w)$ and $d_\Psi(v,w)\geq d_\Phi(v,w)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The subbasis for $\tau_\Phi$ is contained in the subbasis for $\tau_\Psi$, proving
(i).  Equality of the longer signatures implies equality after deleting the
new coordinates, proving (ii).  Inclusion of $\Psi$-signatures implies inclusion
after deleting those coordinates, proving (iii).  The added coordinates make
nonnegative contributions to both distances, proving (iv).
\end{proof}

Adding an observable can split an indistinguishability block, remove a
one-way comparison, and increase measured separation.  A proposed observation
$\psi$ is topologically redundant relative to $\Phi$ exactly when
\[
 \varsigma(\psi)\in\tau_\Phi,
\]
because adding an already open truth region does not refine the topology.
Topological redundancy need not mean numerical redundancy: an added coordinate
can add a further term to $d_\Phi$ and $d_\Phi^+$ while leaving the generated
topology unchanged.  For example, adding $X\wedge Y$ to $\Phi=(X,Y)$ is
topologically redundant because $\varsigma(X\wedge Y)$ is already open.  With
unit weights it nevertheless changes $d^+(B,A)$ from $1$ to $2$.

\subsection{Updating the possible valuations}

Let $S\subseteq\Omega_P$ be the current possibility region.  Learning a
premise $\gamma$ produces
\[
 S\longmapsto S\cap\varsigma(\gamma).
\]
For premises $\Gamma=\{\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_r\}$, define
\[
 S[\Gamma]:=S\cap\bigcap_{j=1}^r\varsigma(\gamma_j),
 \qquad
 S_\Gamma:=\Omega_P[\Gamma].
\]
For an arbitrary current carrier $S$, the updated observation space is
\[
 \mathbf X^\True_{S,\Gamma}
 :=\bigl(S[\Gamma],\tau_\Phi\restr_{S[\Gamma]}\bigr),
 \qquad
 \tau_\Phi\restr_S:=\{U\cap S:U\in\tau_\Phi\}.
\]
When $S=\Omega_P$, write
$\mathbf X^\True_\Gamma:=\mathbf X^\True_{\Omega_P,\Gamma}$.
Sequential updates are associative, commutative, and idempotent because set
intersection has those properties.  Inconsistent premises produce the empty
space.  Smallest neighborhoods restrict accordingly:
\[
 N_{\Phi\mid S[\Gamma]}(v):=S[\Gamma]\cap N_\Phi(v)
 \qquad(v\in S[\Gamma]).
\]

Observation refinement and premise update need not have the same effect.
Refinement changes which distinctions are expressible; update changes which
worlds remain possible.

\section{Inference by truth-region restriction}

Classical inference is a relationship between the common truth region of the
premises and the truth region of the conclusion.

\begin{theorem}[Semantic consequence]
For a finite set of premises $\Gamma$ and a conclusion $\psi$,
\[
 \Gamma\models\psi
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 S_\Gamma\subseteq\varsigma(\psi).
\]
When this holds, the inclusion
\[
 \mathbf X^\True_\Gamma
 \hookrightarrow
 \bigl(\varsigma(\psi),
       \tau_\Phi\restr_{\varsigma(\psi)}\bigr)
\]
is continuous.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The semantic statement says exactly that every valuation satisfying all
premises satisfies $\psi$.  The inclusion between two subspaces of the same
ambient space is continuous.
\end{proof}

The topology contributes a structured representation of this consequence: the
common premise region carries an induced observation topology, and the valid
inclusion is a continuous map into the conclusion subspace.  It does not alter
which consequences are classically valid.  In particular, premise conjunction
uses intersection of truth regions (or the pullback of their induced
subspaces), not intersection of two families of open sets.  The latter is a
different operation: a meet in the lattice of topologies on one fixed carrier.

\subsection{A remark on minimal truth spaces}

For a truth region $S$, one may form the indiscrete space
$\mathcal T^\True_S=(S,\{\varnothing,S\})$.  Intersecting carriers and then
assigning this indiscrete topology transports the ordinary meet
$R\cap S$ of the power set into new notation; it supplies no additional
topological inference principle.  Moreover, $\mathcal T^\True_S$ generally
differs from the induced observation subspace
$(S,\tau_\Phi\restr_S)$, and its inclusion into the ambient observation space
need not be continuous.  It therefore cannot replace the induced subspaces in
the pullback formulation below.  The two spaces coincide exactly when the
induced topology on $S$ is indiscrete, as for a singleton or a region whose
points all have the same observation signature.

\subsection{Modus Ponens and Modus Tollens}

Using $A,B,C,D$,
\begin{align*}
 \varsigma(X\Rightarrow Y)\cap\varsigma(X)
   &=\{B\}
    =\varsigma(X\wedge Y)
    \subseteq\varsigma(Y),\\
 \varsigma(X\Rightarrow Y)\cap\varsigma(\neg Y)
   &=\{D\}
    =\varsigma(\neg X\wedge\neg Y)
    \subseteq\varsigma(\neg X).
\end{align*}
\subsection{Hypothetical Syllogism}

For three variables, the same set semantics gives
\begin{align*}
 \varsigma(X\Rightarrow Y)&=\{B,C,D,F,G,H\},\\
 \varsigma(Y\Rightarrow Z)&=\{A,C,E,F,G,H\},\\
 \varsigma(X\Rightarrow Z)&=\{B,C,E,F,G,H\},
\end{align*}
where $A,\ldots,H$ are the eight complete truth-pattern cells.  Therefore
\[
 \varsigma(X\Rightarrow Y)\cap\varsigma(Y\Rightarrow Z)
 =\{C,F,G,H\}
 \subsetneq\varsigma(X\Rightarrow Z).
\]
The proper inclusion simply records that the two premises carry more
information than the conclusion; validity requires inclusion, not equality.

\subsection{Pullback formulation}

For a single formula $\mathcal L$, write
\[
 \mathbf X^\True_{\mathcal L}
 :=\bigl(\varsigma(\mathcal L),
          \tau_\Phi\restr_{\varsigma(\mathcal L)}\bigr).
\]
The inclusions of two truth subspaces into $(\Omega_P,\tau_\Phi)$ have pullback
\[
 \mathbf X^\True_{\mathcal L_1}
 \times_{(\Omega_P,\tau_\Phi)}
 \mathbf X^\True_{\mathcal L_2}
 \cong
 \mathbf X^\True_{\mathcal L_1\wedge\mathcal L_2}.
\]
For Modus Ponens,
\[
 \mathbf X^\True_{X\Rightarrow Y}
 \times_{(\Omega_{X,Y},\tau_\Phi)}
 \mathbf X^\True_X
 \cong
 \mathbf X^\True_{X\wedge Y}
 \hookrightarrow
 \mathbf X^\True_Y.
\]
Because both arrows are subspace inclusions, this pullback is just the
set-theoretic intersection equipped with its subspace topology, via the
diagonal identification $v\mapsto(v,v)$.  Its universal property is the
standard one for intersections of subspaces: compatible maps into the two
premise regions factor uniquely and continuously through their common region.
Thus the categorical notation repackages premise conjunction; it does not add a
new inference rule.

\section{Continuous maps and preservation of information}

Let $\Phi=(\varphi_i)_{i\in I}$ and $\Psi=(\psi_j)_{j\in J}$ generate the
observation spaces $(\Omega_P,\tau_\Phi)$ and $(\Omega_Q,\tau_\Psi)$.  A map
\[
 f:\Omega_P\longrightarrow\Omega_Q
\]
is continuous when the inverse image of every $\Psi$-observable open event is
$\Phi$-observable.  It suffices to check the subbasic truth regions:
\[
 f^{-1}\bigl(\varsigma(\psi_j)\bigr)\in\tau_\Phi
 \qquad(j\in J).
\]

\begin{proposition}[Monotonicity of continuous maps]
If $f$ is continuous and $v\preceq_\Phi w$, then
\[
 f(v)\preceq_\Psi f(w).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let $U\in\tau_\Psi$ contain $f(v)$.  Then $f^{-1}(U)$ is a $\Phi$-open set
containing $v$, so it contains $w$.  Hence $U$ contains $f(w)$.
\end{proof}

Continuity therefore preserves one-way observational dependence.  This gives
a rigorous starting point for continuous valuation maps.  Conversely, because
these finite spaces have their upper-set topologies, every monotone valuation
map is continuous.  Continuity may collapse distinguishable points and does not
by itself imply preservation of either weighted distance.

\section{Scope, limitations, and deferred directions}

The results above form a finite expository theory of observation,
distinguishability, distance, refinement, and inference.  They do not establish
new homological or application-specific results.  The most direct extensions
are questions about the design and use of observations in reasoning.

\subsection{A presentation-dependent nerve}

A standard relation-nerve construction can be applied to a family of truth
regions.  For an indexed observation family
$\Phi=(\varphi_i)_{i\in I}$, define a simplicial complex
\[
 K_\Phi:=\left\{J\subseteq I:
       \bigcap_{i\in J}\varsigma(\varphi_i)\neq\varnothing
       \right\}.
\]
Its vertices are the indices of individually satisfiable observations, and its
simplices are jointly satisfiable indexed subfamilies.  This is the
observation-side Dowker complex
of the satisfaction relation \cite{Dowker1952}.  It can record higher-order
compatibility not visible from pairwise intersections, but it is not an
invariant of $\tau_\Phi$.  For example,
$\Phi=(X,Y,\neg(X\wedge Y))$ gives the boundary of a triangle.  Its observation
regions are $\{A,B\}$, $\{B,C\}$, and $\{A,C,D\}$: their pairwise intersections
are respectively $\{B\}$, $\{A\}$, and $\{C\}$, while their triple intersection
is empty.  Thus the nerve is connected, whereas the observation space has
connected components $\{B\}$ and $\{A,C,D\}$.  Adjoining a
tautology leaves the generated topology and both signature distances unchanged,
but makes the nerve a cone and kills its reduced homology.  Any homological use
must therefore state the presentation and the intended invariance separately:
the homology of $K_\Phi$ need not agree with the singular homology of the
observation space and is not determined by $\tau_\Phi$.

\subsection{Focused directions beyond the synthesis}

The most natural next step is an observation-design problem rather than a new
name for the finite topology itself: find a smallest or least-cost observation
family that separates designated valuations, certifies a target conclusion, or
distinguishes competing premise sets.  Such questions could support genuinely
new algorithmic or complexity results.  A second direction is to study
sequences in which observation refinement and premise restriction alternate,
or to compare the classical truth-region semantics used here with the Heyting
semantics of the open-set algebra.  These are deliberately left outside the
present expository scope.

\section{Conclusion}

An observation-generated topology can be nontrivial when it records a selected
family of formulas rather than every definable truth set.  Observation
signatures simultaneously determine a partition into indistinguishable states,
a finite topology, and its specialization preorder.  Coordinatewise XOR records
which observations differ; weighted Hamming distance measures symmetric
disagreement; and the directed distance $d_\Phi^+$ measures loss of positive
information while generating the selected observation topology.  Adding tests
refines distinguishability, while adding premises restricts the possibility
space.  Inference is the inclusion of that restricted region in the truth
region of a conclusion.

The framework gives a common notation for partitioning, distinguishability,
asymmetric separation, logical distance, and refinement.  Its individual
ingredients are classical.  Its value here is expository: it makes explicit
which structures are determined by the observations, which require extra
weights or presentation choices, and which logical claims remain ordinary
model-set inclusions.  Natural research extensions would add an algorithmic or
complexity result, a new invariant, or a validated application rather than more
renamings of the same finite structures.

# Next Research Gate — Interaction-Core Spectral Sequence Beyond Matching

**Project:** Mathematical Reconstruction of Matte-Blanco's Unfolding Function and Mental Space  
**Thread:** Observation refinement, carrier splitting, higher-dimensional inversion complexes

## Required starting materials

Use this consolidated package as the authoritative project handoff. Before beginning, read:

1. `00_START_HERE/MASTER_HANDOFF.md`;
2. `00_START_HERE/CLAIM_STATUS_MATRIX.md`;
3. `02_LATEST_HIGHER_DIMENSIONAL_GATE/EXACT_THEOREMS_AND_PROOFS.md`;
4. `02_LATEST_HIGHER_DIMENSIONAL_GATE/COUNTEREXAMPLES_AND_OBSTRUCTIONS.md`;

The latest files supersede earlier formulations where they differ.

Act as an independent mathematical research panel specializing in finite posets, combinatorial topology, spectral sequences, discrete Morse theory, relative simplicial homology, graph/biclique structure, homotopy colimits, integer Smith normal form, and algorithmic topology.

This is a theorem-discovery gate, not an editorial pass.

Your task is to determine whether the **interaction-core filtration** of the higher-dimensional carrier-splitting inversion complex admits a second exact theorem beyond the exclusive-inversion matching case.

Do not optimize for a positive result.

---

## 1. Frozen baseline

Let `Q` be the old finite observational `T0` poset and let a new Boolean observation give `Q^psi subset Q x {0,1}`.

Let:

- `P` = 1-only coarse states;
- `Z` = 0-only coarse states;
- `C` = genuinely split states.

Define the exclusive inversion graph

`G_psi = (P sqcup Z, E_psi)`

with

`E_psi = {(p,z): p<z in Q}`.

In the full doubled product `D=Q x {0<1}`, let `K=Delta D` and let `L=Delta Q^psi` be the induced complex after deleting the missing lower copies of `P` and missing upper copies of `Z`.

The mapping-cone defect is represented by the relative pair `(K,L)`.

The latest gate proved:

### Matching theorem

If `G_psi` is a matching, then for every coefficient ring `R`,

`H_n(Cone(Delta pi);R) ~= direct_sum_{(p,z) in E_psi} H~_{n-2}(lk_{Delta Q}[p,z];R)`.

This theorem is frozen.

### Sharp failure of forest extension

The coarse chain `0<1<2` with `(1-only,0-only,0-only)` has exclusive graph `K_{1,2}` but produces `H~_1 ~= Z` even though the independent edge-link sum vanishes.

Therefore any theorem beyond matching must explicitly account for **shared-endpoint/higher-core interactions**.

---

## 2. Interaction-core filtration

For a relative simplex `sigma`, define its missing/interacting core `S(sigma)` to be the subset of missing vertices contained in `sigma`.

Filter the relative chain complex by core size:

`F_r C_* = span{sigma : |S(sigma)| <= r}`.

The associated graded complex is already known to decompose over mixed cores into shifted available-link complexes. Mixed cores are precisely **chain-supported bicliques** of the exclusive inversion graph.

Your first task is to reconstruct this filtration carefully, fix indexing/sign conventions, and write the spectral sequence explicitly, including the `E^0`, `E^1`, and the first potentially nonzero interaction differential.

Do not claim novelty for the general filtered-complex spectral-sequence machinery.

---

## 3. Primary structural classes to attack

Investigate these in parallel before committing to one.

### Class A — maximum degree at most 2

`G_psi` is a disjoint union of paths and even cycles.

Questions:

- Does the core-size spectral sequence collapse at `E^2`?
- Can the `d^1` differential be written explicitly as a signed incidence operator between edge-link and 3-vertex-core link groups?
- For a path component, is cone homology computable by an iterated mapping cone / chain complex of coarse-link homology groups?
- What new phenomenon occurs on the first cycle?
- Is there an exact necessary-and-sufficient acyclicity criterion?

The two-edge star counterexample must appear as the first nonmatching local model and must be recovered by the formula.

### Class B — Ferrers exclusive inversion graphs

Test whether nested neighborhoods force a tractable core poset or a spectral-sequence collapse.

Search for formulas in terms of:

- maximal bicliques;
- Ferrers diagrams;
- intervals/links in `Q`;
- Möbius functions;
- cellular resolutions or order-complex decompositions.

### Class C — chordal-bipartite exclusive inversion graphs

Determine whether the absence of induced cycles longer than 4 gives a recursive decomposition by bisimplicial edges/vertices.

Test whether this yields:

- an exact homology recursion;
- a discrete Morse matching;
- a collapse theorem;
- or merely an algorithmic decomposition.

### Class D — bounded biclique/core size

If every chain-supported mixed core has size at most `r`, determine whether the interaction spectral sequence is concentrated in a bounded range and whether this forces collapse at a bounded page.

A useful result could be of the form:

`max mixed core size <= r  =>  E^{r}=E^infinity`

but do not assume this is true.

---

## 4. Algebraic target

Try to replace the matching direct sum by a small explicit **interaction chain complex** whose terms are coarse-link homology groups indexed by mixed cores.

A desired form is schematically:

`I_p = direct_sum_{|S|=p+2} H~_{*-shift(S)}(Lambda_S)`

with boundary maps induced by deletion of one missing vertex/core incidence.

Prove whether the spectral sequence collapses so that the homology of this interaction chain complex is the actual cone homology on one of the target structural classes.

A theorem of this type would be stronger than a generic fiber criterion because it would compute the nontrivial cases rather than merely recognize homotopy equivalences.

---

Completely classify the smallest interacting exclusive graphs:

1. `K_{1,2}` and `K_{2,1}` stars;
2. path of three exclusive edges;
3. `K_{2,2}`;
4. first chordal-bipartite but non-Ferrers example;
5. first even-cycle interaction.

For each, derive a chain-level formula in terms of coarse links/intersections and compare with direct integral SNF.

Identify which local model first supports:

- a nonzero interaction differential;
- torsion produced by interaction rather than inherited from a link;
- a higher differential `d^r`, `r>=2`;
- noncollapse at `E^2`.

---

## 6. Controlled computational discovery

Build on the existing scripts rather than starting over.

At minimum:

- enumerate/deduplicate coarse posets through the next feasible size;
- enumerate availability profiles;
- compute exact integral cone homology via Smith normal form;
- build the exclusive graph and mixed-core poset;
- compute the interaction filtration and spectral-sequence pages algorithmically where feasible;
- group cases by exclusive graph isomorphism type;
- search separately within max-degree-2, Ferrers, and chordal-bipartite classes;
- find minimal counterexamples to every candidate collapse theorem;
- distinguish torsion inherited from coarse links from torsion created by interaction differentials.

Preserve machine-readable CSV/JSON outputs.

---

## 7. Priority/literature gate

Before declaring a theorem novel, search through 2026 for close results on:

- vertex-cover obstruction complexes;
- multi-vertex deletion cofibers;
- Mayer–Vietoris/Čech spectral sequences for vertex deletions;
- homotopy colimits indexed by biclique posets;
- Ferrers/chordal-bipartite independence/order complexes;
- spectral sequences of filtered relative simplicial complexes;
- poset fiber decompositions;
- discrete Morse theory for bipartite/Ferrers structures;
- biclique complexes and Dowker-type constructions.

In particular, compare every proposed theorem with Chachólski–Jin–Scolamiero–Tombari and Björner–Wachs–Welker rather than merely citing them in background.

For each theorem state explicitly:

- standard ingredient;
- closest prior theorem;
- project-specific additional content;
- confidence in priority.

---

## 8. Adversarial review

Run at least these attacks after finding a candidate theorem:

1. **spectral-sequence referee** — attacks indexing, convergence, extensions, and hidden higher differentials;
2. **combinatorial topology referee** — seeks a standard obstruction-complex reformulation;
3. **integer homology referee** — searches for torsion and coefficient dependence;
4. **graph theorist** — tests whether Ferrers/chordal/max-degree hypotheses are really natural and correctly characterized;
5. **hostile counterexample search** — find the smallest case violating the proposed formula.

Do not update the main manuscript until the theorem survives these attacks.

---

## 9. Gate success levels

### Level A — Strong success
A natural interacting class admits a necessary-and-sufficient exact formula/classification, with proof and computational verification.

### Level B — Significant success
A natural class admits an explicit interaction-chain complex plus a proved spectral-sequence collapse / exact recursion that computes the cone.

### Level C — Useful partial success
The spectral sequence is made explicit and useful sufficient conditions/collapse bounds are proved, but no closed classification.

### Level D — Negative but informative
The target classes fail, with minimal counterexamples and a clear obstruction hierarchy.

### Level E — Standard theory only
Nothing materially improves known generic obstruction/fiber machinery.

---

Produce:

- `INTERACTION_CORE_RESEARCH_GATE.md`

Only if the gate reaches Level A or B, also produce a manuscript-ready LaTeX section. Do **not** overwrite the v0.3 baseline.

---

## 11. Final questions

End by answering:

1. Does a second exact theorem exist beyond matching?
2. Which structural class gives the strongest result?
3. What is the exact spectral sequence / interaction complex?
4. Does it collapse at `E^2`, and under exactly what hypotheses?
5. How does it recover empty-graph neutrality and the matching theorem?

9. Is the theorem genuinely stronger than standard obstruction-complex or poset-fiber theory?
10. Should it be merged into the current paper, or reserved for a second paper?
11. What single theorem should be attacked next?

The final verdict must be conservative and theorem-level.

# MASTER HANDOFF — Unfolding / Observation-Refinement / Carrier-Splitting Program

**Date:** 29 September 2026  
**Status:** Active research program. Latest gate reached **Level A mathematically** on a restricted natural class. Publication-level novelty remains subject to conservative theorem-level priority review.

---

## A. Research arc to date

### Phase 0 — historical recovery from the thesis

The 2015 thesis proposed:

- Mental Space as a topological representation of the mind;
- concepts as simplicial complexes;
- a logical "distinguishing/unfolding" operator `partial` intended to decompose concepts;
- gluing/integration back to larger concepts;
- cycles/boundaries as possible symmetry/asymmetry indicators;
- ProLT/presheaf/exact-sequence/homology analogies.

The audit found a real mathematical seed but also important defects:

- the thesis unfolding operator is not the genuine simplicial boundary;
- it is presentation-sensitive as a Boolean operator;
- its repeated application is better understood through Boolean/Hamming layers;
- the printed gluing identity is not generally correct;
- cycles do not characterize symmetry;
- the thesis's topology/homology analogies require principled reconstruction.

See `05_ORIGINAL_UNFOLDING_AUDIT/`.

### Phase 1 — two-operator modern model

The project separated:

- `d`, the genuine chain differential with `d^2=0`;
- `U_k`, an unfolding/refinement map between complexes/stages.

If `U_k` is induced by a simplicial map, `d U_k = U_k d`, so refinement induces homology maps. Mapping cones and relative homology became the natural measures of structural change.

The old simplex notes also led to an exact Hamming-layer viewpoint and a cumulative skeleton filtration. See `04_OBSERVATION_REFINEMENT_DRAFT/`.

### Phase 2 — observation-refinement descent and cone theorem

For compatible observational covers/refinements, the project formulated mapping-cone defects and descent/reconstruction defects. The key conceptual split became:

- **structural change:** `H_*(Cone U)`;
- **reconstruction failure:** kernel/cokernel of the restriction-to-compatible-local-data map.

This phase also replaced "cycles = symmetry" with a distinct observational symmetry group, whose invisible transformations can only shrink under finer observations.

### Phase 3 — carrier splitting

The major issue was what happens when a new observation splits one old `T0` observational state into multiple refined states.

Let `Q` be the old finite observational poset and `Q^psi subset Q x {0,1}` the refined carrier. The carrier-splitting gate proved:

1. Introduce a split completion `Qhat^psi` that duplicates/splits the carrier but retains all old coarse comparisons.
2. `Qhat^psi -> Q` is homotopy-neutral (beat-point reduction).
3. The actual refined order `Q^psi` is obtained from `Qhat^psi` by one-bit monotonicity thinning.
4. Therefore carrier splitting is **neutral blow-up + order defect**.
5. The cone homology is the relative homology `H_*(Delta Qhat^psi, Delta Q^psi)`.
6. Relative chains are exactly split-completion chains whose bit-word contains a descent `1...0`.

For weighted height `<=2`, the gate obtained a complete integral rooted-incidence classification and a total-unimodularity result. Above that height, unrestricted torsion/universality forbids a universal rooted-forest criterion.

See `03_CARRIER_SPLITTING_GATE/`.

### Phase 4 — higher-dimensional inversion complex

The latest gate changed to a full-doubling model:

`D = Q x {0<1}`,

with the actual refined carrier obtained by deleting missing copies:

- `(p,0)` for 1-only states `p`;
- `(z,1)` for 0-only states `z`.

This converts carrier splitting into a highly structured two-colour vertex-deletion problem in `Delta(Q x 2)`.

Define the **exclusive inversion graph**

`G_psi = (P sqcup Z, E_psi)`,

`E_psi = {(p,z): p in P, z in Z, p < z}`.

Every mixed relative simplex has a missing-core whose endpoints form a chain-supported biclique of this graph.

---

## B. Strongest current theorem

### Exclusive-Inversion Matching Theorem

If `E_psi` is a matching, then for every integer `n` and every coefficient ring `R`,

`H_n(Cone(Delta pi);R)`

is naturally isomorphic to

`direct_sum_{(p,z) in E_psi} H~_{n-2}(lk_{Delta Q}[p,z];R)`.

Consequences:

- exact all-dimensional classification on this class;
- integral torsion is retained and computed from the edge links;
- homology equivalence occurs iff every relevant coarse edge link is acyclic (with chosen coefficients);
- for a bounded coarse poset, only the global endpoint inversion can contribute;
- endpoint profiles on finite distributive lattices are neutral except for Boolean lattices, where the cone has a single top-dimensional `Z` class;
- arbitrary finite-poset reduced homology can be shifted by two degrees into a one-edge matching carrier-split system.

Formal proofs are in `02_LATEST_HIGHER_DIMENSIONAL_GATE/EXACT_THEOREMS_AND_PROOFS.md`.

---

## C. Why the theorem works

Two separate colour deletions are individually homotopy-neutral. Their mixed interaction is where the defect lives. Under the matching hypothesis, every relative simplex contains exactly one missing lower/upper pair, so the relative chain complex splits directly over exclusive inversion edges.

Each fixed-edge summand is the augmented chain complex of the product-edge link, shifted. The product-edge link is homotopy equivalent to a suspension of the corresponding coarse edge link. This yields the formula above.

This is stronger/more explicit than merely applying a generic fiber-contractibility criterion, but it is structurally close to classical vertex-deletion/cofiber and obstruction-complex theory. Priority claims must reflect that.

---

## D. Sharp failures / boundaries

### D1. Forest is not enough

The coarse chain `0<1<2` with availability `(1-only, 0-only, 0-only)` has exclusive inversion graph `K_{1,2}`, a forest. Yet the actual cone has `H~_1 ~= Z`, while summing individual edge-link contributions gives zero.

Thus the first shared endpoint creates a genuine 3-vertex interaction core.

### D2. Matching does not imply torsion-free or TU

Let `Q = 0hat + R + 1hat`, take only the endpoint inversion, and split every state of `R`. The exclusive graph is one edge but

`H_n(Cone;Z) ~= H~_{n-2}(Delta R;Z)`.

Arbitrary torsion can therefore occur inside the matching class.

### D3. Horn is mainly neutral in the strongest relational form

A nonempty meet-closed full refined relation has a minimum; its projection is also meet-closed with a minimum. Both order complexes are contractible. Dual-Horn is dual.

### D4. Universal all-height graph criteria are impossible

The companion one-bit thinning theory already permits torsion and very general homotopy behavior. Carrier splitting contains that regime. Any further theorem must impose real structural restrictions.

---

## E. Interaction-core filtration: current open frontier

For a relative simplex `sigma`, let `S(sigma)` be the set of missing vertices it contains. Filtering the relative complex by `|S(sigma)|` gives an associated graded complex indexed by mixed missing cores. These cores correspond to chain-supported bicliques of the exclusive inversion graph.

- no exclusive edges -> isotone-section neutrality;
- matching -> only 2-vertex mixed cores -> exact direct-sum edge-link theorem;
- a star -> 3-vertex cores appear -> first nontrivial interactions/differentials;
- larger bicliques -> higher interaction levels.

This hierarchy is the key to the next theorem.

---

## F. Computational evidence already obtained

Latest higher-dimensional gate:

- 3,242 matching cases through 4 coarse states checked integrally by Smith normal form: 0 formula failures;
- 1,707 product-edge link-suspension checks through 5 states: 0 failures;
- 639 additional nonempty-matching 5-state cases checked over `F_2`: 0 failures;
- Horn/dual-Horn closure families exhaustively checked through 4 refined coordinates;
- small finite distributive-lattice endpoint cases checked integrally.

Earlier carrier-splitting gate:

- 3,450 poset/profile cases through 4 coarse states;
- 2,172 weighted-height `<=2` cases all agreed with the rooted-incidence theorem;
- mapping-cone and relative split-completion computations agreed in every tested case.

All scripts/results are included.

---

## G. Literature and novelty boundary

Established ingredients that must be credited:

- Stong: finite `T0` spaces / beat points;
- Quillen/Barmak: poset-fiber criteria and simple-homotopy refinements;
- Björner–Wachs–Welker: poset-fiber homotopy decompositions;
- Fernández–Minian: relation/mapping-cylinder constructions in finite posets;
- Chachólski–Jin–Scolamiero–Tombari: vertex-cover obstruction complexes and homotopical decompositions;
- Dey–Hirani–Krishnamoorthy: total unimodularity vs torsion in relative simplicial pairs;
- classical crosscut/distributive-lattice topology;
- classical Horn/intersection-closure theory.

Current defensible candidate contribution:

> A Boolean observation split becomes a special two-colour missing-copy problem in `Delta(Q x 2)`. The 1-only-to-0-only comparison graph organizes the interactions. When that graph is a matching, the relative chain complex separates and yields an exact all-dimensional integral coarse-edge-link formula.

Do **not** claim a new general theory of vertex deletion, cofibers, nerves, or poset fibers.

---

## H. Manuscript status and merge policy

Current baseline manuscript:

`01_CURRENT_MANUSCRIPT/Observation_Refinement_Descent_and_Cone_Draft_v0.3.tex`

Latest theorem insertion prepared but not merged:

`01_CURRENT_MANUSCRIPT/MANUSCRIPT_REVISION_SECTION.tex`

Recommended policy:

1. keep v0.3 frozen as baseline;
2. run the next interaction-core research gate;
3. if the next gate yields Level A/B, decide whether matching + interacting theorem form one coherent paper;
4. then merge and run a hostile proof/priority/editorial pass;
5. only after that produce a submission candidate.

---

## I. Next research theorem

The next target is not another generic carrier-splitting theorem. It is:

### Interaction-Core Spectral Sequence Classification Beyond Matching

Start with exclusive inversion graphs having controlled overlap, especially:

- maximum degree `<=2` (paths/cycles);
- Ferrers bipartite graphs;
- chordal-bipartite graphs;
- bounded biclique/core size.

Determine whether the core-size filtration spectral sequence collapses at `E^2` and give exact formulas for the differentials/homology from coarse links plus overlap data.

A successful theorem should recover:

- empty graph neutrality;

- the two-edge star counterexample as the first nontrivial interaction term.

The full research prompt is `00_START_HERE/NEXT_RESEARCH_PROMPT.md`.

---

## J. What the next agent should NOT do first

Do not immediately rewrite the paper. Do not restart the thesis audit. Do not rerun only the same small computations. Do not broaden into generic cognition/topology literature before understanding the exact current theorem hierarchy.

First verify the baseline theorem statements, then attack the next interaction-core gate.

# Higher-Dimensional Inversion Complex Classification Gate

**Project:** Mathematical Reconstruction of Matte-Blanco's Unfolding Function and Mental Space  
**Date:** 29 September 2026  
**Gate verdict:** **LEVEL A -- STRONG SUCCESS, with a conservative priority qualification.**

The gate found an exact all-dimensional **integral homology classification** on a natural noninteraction class: carrier-splitting systems whose **exclusive inversion graph is a matching**.  The classification is not restricted by height.  It can produce homology in arbitrarily high degree and can transfer torsion.  A second exact corollary gives a particularly clean Boolean/distributive-lattice classification.  The underlying simplicial deletion/cofiber technology has substantial prior art, so the publication claim should be the specialized observation-theoretic recognition and exact link formula, not the generic topology of deleting vertices.

---

## 1. Frozen setting

Let `Q` be a finite observational `T0` poset and let a new Boolean observation `psi` produce a refined carrier

\[
Q^\psi\subseteq Q\times\{0,1\},
\]

ordered by the product order.  Write

\[
A_a=\{s\in Q:(s,a)\in Q^\psi\},\qquad a\in\{0,1\}.
\]

Separate the coarse states into

\[
P=A_1\setminus A_0 \quad\text{(1-only)},\qquad
Z=A_0\setminus A_1 \quad\text{(0-only)},\qquad
C=A_0\cap A_1 \quad\text{(split)}.
\]

The preceding carrier-splitting gate used a split completion `Qhat^psi`.  The present gate found a second, more useful all-height model.

---

## 2. Full-doubling / missing-copy model

Let

\[
D=Q\times\mathbf 2,
\qquad K=\Delta D,
\qquad L=\Delta Q^\psi.
\]

The actual refined carrier is obtained from `D` by deleting exactly

\[
M_0=\{(p,0):p\in P\},
\qquad
M_1=\{(z,1):z\in Z\}.
\]

Thus `L` is the induced subcomplex of `K` on the remaining vertices.

The projection

\[
D\longrightarrow Q
\]

is a homotopy equivalence: it has both the bottom-row and top-row closure sections.  Consequently the homotopy cofiber of

\[
\Delta\pi:\Delta Q^\psi\to\Delta Q
\]

has the same reduced homology as the relative pair

\[
H_*(K,L;R).
\]

This model is useful because carrier splitting becomes a very special **two-colour vertex deletion problem** from the product order complex `Delta(Q x 2)`.

---

## 3. General two-colour deletion square

Delete the two kinds of missing vertices separately:

\[
K_P=K[V(K)\setminus M_0],
\qquad
K_Z=K[V(K)\setminus M_1],
\]

and put

\[
U=K_P\cup K_Z,
\qquad
L=K_P\cap K_Z.
\]

`K_P` retracts by the ascending closure operator `(s,a) -> (s,1)` to the full top row, while `K_Z` retracts by the descending closure operator `(s,a) -> (s,0)` to the full bottom row.  Hence both inclusions

\[
K_P\hookrightarrow K,
\qquad
K_Z\hookrightarrow K
\]

are homotopy equivalences.

The long exact sequences of triples plus simplicial excision therefore give, for every coefficient ring `R`,

\[
\boxed{
H_n(K,L;R)\cong H_{n+1}(K,U;R).
}
\tag{3.1}
\]

This is the fundamental algebraic reduction of the new gate.

A simplex lies in `K \ U` exactly when it contains **at least one missing lower copy** `(p,0)`, `p in P`, and **at least one missing upper copy** `(z,1)`, `z in Z`.

---

## 4. Exclusive inversion graph

Define the bipartite graph

\[
G_\psi=(P\sqcup Z,E_\psi),
\qquad
E_\psi=\{(p,z)\in P\times Z:p<z\text{ in }Q\}.
\]

Call it the **exclusive inversion graph**.

It records exactly the places where a coarse comparison tries to run from a state where only outcome `1` is available to a later state where only outcome `0` is available.

For every relative simplex `sigma in K \ U`, let

\[
P(\sigma)=\{p\in P:(p,0)\in\sigma\},
\qquad
Z(\sigma)=\{z\in Z:(z,1)\in\sigma\}.
\]

Because `sigma` is a chain in `Q x 2`,

\[
P(\sigma)\times Z(\sigma)\subseteq E_\psi.
\]

Thus every higher interaction in the relative complex is supported on a **biclique** of the exclusive inversion graph.  This is the structural reason a matching is special: it forbids every mixed core larger than one edge.

---

## 5. Exact all-height theorem

### Theorem -- Exclusive-Inversion Matching Theorem

Assume that `E_psi` is a matching; equivalently, every `1`-only state and every `0`-only state participates in at most one exclusive inversion.

Then for every integer `n` and every coefficient ring `R`,

\[
\boxed{
H_n\!\left(\operatorname{Cone}(\Delta\pi);R\right)
\cong
\bigoplus_{(p,z)\in E_\psi}
\widetilde H_{n-2}\!\left(
\operatorname{lk}_{\Delta Q}[p,z];R
\right).
}
\tag{5.1}
\]

In particular, integrally,

\[
\boxed{
H_n\!\left(\operatorname{Cone}(\Delta\pi);\mathbb Z\right)
\cong
\bigoplus_{(p,z)\in E_\psi}
\widetilde H_{n-2}\!\left(
\operatorname{lk}_{\Delta Q}[p,z];\mathbb Z
\right).
}
\tag{5.2}
\]

The theorem is a complete homology classification on this class: Betti numbers and torsion are read off from coarse **edge links**.

### Immediate necessary-and-sufficient homological criterion

Under the matching hypothesis, the carrier split is an integral homology equivalence iff every relevant coarse edge link is integrally acyclic:

\[
\Delta\pi\text{ is a homology equivalence}
\iff
\widetilde H_*(\operatorname{lk}_{\Delta Q}[p,z];\mathbb Z)=0
\quad\forall(p,z)\in E_\psi.
\]

The same statement holds over any chosen coefficient field/ring with that coefficient system substituted.

---

## 6. Proof of the matching theorem

### 6.1 Unique mixed core

A simplex in `K \ U` contains at least one vertex `(p,0)` with `p in P` and one vertex `(z,1)` with `z in Z`.  Any such pair in the same product-order chain satisfies `p<z`, hence gives an edge of `E_psi`.

If a relative simplex contained two different missing lower vertices and one missing upper vertex, the latter would have degree at least two in `E_psi`.  Dually, two missing upper vertices and one missing lower vertex would force degree at least two on the lower endpoint.  Therefore, when `E_psi` is a matching, every simplex in `K \ U` contains a **unique** pair

\[
e=((p,0)<(z,1)),\qquad (p,z)\in E_\psi.
\]

### 6.2 Chain-level direct sum

The relative chain complex consequently splits:

\[
C_m(K,U;R)
=\bigoplus_{e\in E_\psi} C_m^{(e)}.
\]

For a fixed edge `e`, every relative simplex is uniquely `e union tau` with `tau` a simplex in `lk_K(e)`.  Deleting either endpoint of `e` lands in `U` and is zero in the relative quotient; deleting a vertex of `tau` remains in the same `e`-summand.  Hence, up to the harmless orientation sign,

\[
C_m^{(e)}\cong \widetilde C_{m-2}(\operatorname{lk}_K e).
\]

Thus

\[
H_m(K,U;R)
\cong
\bigoplus_{e\in E_\psi}
\widetilde H_{m-2}(\operatorname{lk}_K e;R).
\tag{6.1}
\]

Combining (3.1) and (6.1),

\[
H_n(K,L;R)
\cong
\bigoplus_{e\in E_\psi}
\widetilde H_{n-1}(\operatorname{lk}_K e;R).
\tag{6.2}
\]

### 6.3 Product-edge link is a suspension of the coarse edge link

For `e=((p,0)<(z,1))`, the product edge link decomposes as

\[
\operatorname{lk}_{\Delta(Q\times\mathbf2)}e
=
\Delta(Q_{<p}) * \Delta M_{p,z} * \Delta(Q_{>z}),
\]

where

\[
M_{p,z}=((p,0),(z,1))_{Q\times\mathbf2}.
\]

Let `R=(p,z)_Q`.  The middle poset consists of `(p,1)`, `R x 2`, and `(z,0)`.  Remove `(z,0)`: the result closes upward onto the bit-1 row and has minimum `(p,1)`, hence is contractible.  Remove `(p,1)`: the result closes downward onto the bit-0 row and has maximum `(z,0)`, hence is contractible.  Their intersection is `R x 2`, homotopy equivalent to `R`.  Since `(p,1)` and `(z,0)` are incomparable, these two subcomplexes cover the middle order complex.  Therefore

\[
\Delta M_{p,z}\simeq \Sigma\Delta(p,z)_Q.
\]

Consequently

\[
\operatorname{lk}_{\Delta(Q\times\mathbf2)}e
\simeq
\Sigma\,\operatorname{lk}_{\Delta Q}[p,z].
\tag{6.3}
\]

Applying reduced homology to (6.2) and (6.3) proves (5.1).

---

## 7. Exact neutrality before the first inversion

The exclusive graph also gives a clean zeroth obstruction.

### Proposition -- isotone extension criterion

If `E_psi` is empty, then `Delta pi` is a homotopy equivalence.

Indeed, the prescribed partial Boolean labeling

- `b(p)=1` on `P`,
- `b(z)=0` on `Z`,

extends monotonically to all of `Q` iff there is no `p in P`, `z in Z` with `p<z`.  One explicit extension is

\[
b(s)=1 \iff \exists p\in P\text{ with }p\le s.
\]

The section `r(s)=(s,b(s))` satisfies `pi r=id_Q`.  Define

\[
c_+(s,a)=(s,\max\{a,b(s)\}).
\]

Then

\[
\operatorname{id}_{Q^\psi}\le c_+\ge r\pi,
\]

so `r pi` is homotopic to the identity through comparable monotone maps.

Thus a nonempty exclusive inversion graph is a necessary condition for a carrier-splitting homotopy defect.

---

## 8. General interaction-core filtration

The matching theorem is the collapse case of a broader all-height filtration.

For `sigma in K \ U`, define its **missing core**

\[
S(\sigma)=\sigma\cap(M_0\cup M_1).
\]

It contains vertices of both colours.  Filter the relative complex `C_*(K,U)` by core cardinality:

\[
F_r C_m
=
\langle\sigma:\ |S(\sigma)|\le r\rangle,
\qquad r\ge2.
\]

The boundary cannot increase the core size.  Let `C_r` denote the set of `r`-vertex mixed missing cores that are simplices of `K`, and for `S in C_r` let

\[
\Lambda_S
=
\operatorname{lk}_K(S)[V(L)]
\]

be the part of the link supported on available vertices.  Then

\[
\operatorname{gr}_r C_m(K,U)
\cong
\bigoplus_{S\in\mathcal C_r}
\widetilde C_{m-r}(\Lambda_S).
\tag{8.1}
\]

Hence there is a convergent spectral sequence whose first page is assembled from

\[
\widetilde H_*(\Lambda_S)
\]

indexed by mixed missing cores.  Every core projects to a chain-supported biclique of `G_psi`; differentials between filtration levels are exactly the interactions produced by deleting missing vertices.

For a matching there are no mixed cores with more than two vertices, so the filtration collapses immediately and gives Theorem (5.1).  For the old weighted-height-at-most-two regime, the only surviving core interactions are deleted edge/triangle incidences; the former rooted-incidence graph is the low-dimensional shadow of this filtration.

This filtration is the strongest general result found at this gate outside the exact matching class.  It is useful, but it is not advertised as a closed higher-dimensional classification.

---

## 9. Bounded-poset and Boolean/distributive corollaries

Assume `Q` has a least element `0hat` and greatest element `1hat` and the exclusive inversion graph is a matching.

For a coarse edge `p<z`,

\[
\operatorname{lk}_{\Delta Q}[p,z]
=
\Delta(Q_{<p})*\Delta(p,z)*\Delta(Q_{>z}).
\]

If `p != 0hat`, the first factor has a minimum and is contractible.  If `z != 1hat`, the last factor has a maximum and is contractible.  Therefore **only the global endpoint inversion can contribute**:

\[
H_n(\operatorname{Cone}\Delta\pi;\mathbb Z)
\cong
\begin{cases}
\widetilde H_{n-2}(\Delta(Q\setminus\{\hat0,\hat1\});\mathbb Z),
& \hat0\in P,\ \hat1\in Z,\\
0,&\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\tag{9.1}
\]

### Finite distributive lattices

Let `Q=L=J(R)` be a finite distributive lattice.  By the crosscut theorem, together with the standard atom structure of `J(R)`, the proper-part order complex is

- contractible if `R` is not an antichain;
- a sphere `S^{r-2}` if `R` is an `r`-element antichain, equivalently `L=B_r` is Boolean.

Therefore, under the endpoint matching profile,

\[
H_n(\operatorname{Cone}\Delta\pi;\mathbb Z)
\cong
\begin{cases}
\mathbb Z,&L=B_r\text{ and }n=r,\\
0,&\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\tag{9.2}
\]

This gives genuine higher-dimensional examples:

\[
B_2\rightsquigarrow H_2\cong\mathbb Z,
\qquad
B_3\rightsquigarrow H_3\cong\mathbb Z,
\qquad
B_4\rightsquigarrow H_4\cong\mathbb Z.
\]

The first two were checked directly by integral Smith-normal-form computation; the `B_4` result follows from the theorem and was checked through the link formula.

---

## 10. Horn and dual-Horn regimes

A different conclusion holds when the **entire refined signature relation** is Horn.

If `Q^psi` is a nonempty meet-closed subset of a Boolean cube, then it has a least element (the meet of all realized refined signatures).  Its coordinate projection `Q` is also meet-closed, hence also has a least element.  Both order complexes are contractible, so

\[
\Delta\pi:\Delta Q^\psi\to\Delta Q
\]

is a homotopy equivalence.

Dually, a nonempty join-closed refined relation has a greatest element, as does its projection, and is again homotopy-neutral.

Thus **pure Horn/dual-Horn closure does not generate a nontrivial carrier-splitting defect**.  It is a useful exact neutral class, not the source of the desired higher-dimensional topology.

This is deliberately narrower than the companion paper's Horn-type repair criterion: it assumes closure of the full refined realized-signature relation itself, not merely that one truth region of an arbitrary observation is Horn-definable.

---

## 11. Torsion and universality inside the exact matching class

The matching condition controls **interaction between inversion defects**, not the topology of the coarse edge links.

Let `R` be any nonempty finite poset.  Form

\[
Q=\hat0\oplus R\oplus\hat1
\]

by adjoining a global bottom and top.  Make `0hat` 1-only, `1hat` 0-only, and every state of `R` genuinely split.  Then

\[
E_\psi=\{(\hat0,\hat1)\}
\]

is a one-edge matching and

\[
\operatorname{lk}_{\Delta Q}[\hat0,\hat1]=\Delta R.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
H_n(\operatorname{Cone}\Delta\pi;\mathbb Z)
\cong
\widetilde H_{n-2}(\Delta R;\mathbb Z).
}
\tag{11.1}
\]

Consequences:

1. nonzero cone homology occurs in arbitrarily high degree inside the matching class;
2. arbitrary integral torsion occurring in finite-poset homology transfers two degrees upward;
3. a universal wedge-of-spheres theorem is false even under exclusive-inversion matching;
4. matching does **not** imply total unimodularity.

For example, using a finite-poset model of `RP^2` as `R` yields `Z/2` torsion in cone degree 3.  The 13-point projective-plane model cited in the companion paper gives a small explicit construction after adjoining the two endpoints, but minimality in the matching class is not claimed here.

---

## 12. Sharp failure outside the matching hypothesis

The smallest possible nonmatching exclusive graph already destroys naive edgewise additivity.

Take the three-element chain

\[
0<1<2
\]

with availability profile

\[
(\{1\},\{0\},\{0\}).
\]

Then

\[
E_\psi=\{(0,1),(0,2)\},
\]

a two-edge star, hence a forest but not a matching.

Direct integral computation gives

\[
H_1(\operatorname{Cone}\Delta\pi;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z.
\]

However both individual coarse edge links are contractible, so the naive sum of the matching formula predicts zero.

The missing 2-simplex containing `(0,0),(1,1),(2,1)` couples the two inversion edges.  Therefore:

\[
\boxed{\text{``exclusive inversion graph is a forest'' is not enough.}}
\]

Three coarse states are minimal for this failure because a nonmatching bipartite graph needs at least three incident vertices.

---

## 13. Total-unimodularity boundary

The earlier height-two theorem had a TU relative boundary matrix because its columns were signed graph-incidence columns.

That phenomenon does not survive the present all-height class.  Dey--Hirani--Krishnamoorthy characterize TU of a simplicial boundary matrix by torsion-freeness of a whole family of pure relative subcomplex pairs, not merely by torsion-freeness of one global homology group.  The matching realization (11.1) transfers arbitrary torsion, so matching cannot imply TU.

Even when every edge link is torsion-free and the cone homology is therefore free, that alone is insufficient to claim TU of all inversion boundary matrices.  No new all-dimensional forbidden-minor characterization of TU was established at this gate.

**Verdict for the TU program:** useful negative boundary, not a new TU theorem.

---

## 14. Computational evidence

The new verifier `verify_matching_inversion_theorem.py` performs exact integral Smith-normal-form computations on the full doubled-product relative pair.

### Exhaustive results

Across every naturally labelled finite coarse poset on at most four states and all fiber profiles `{0}`, `{1}`, `{0,1}`:

- **3,450** poset/profile cases were examined;
- **3,242** satisfied the exclusive-inversion matching condition and were checked integrally by Smith normal form;
- **566** of those had at least one exclusive inversion edge;
- **0** failures of formula (5.2) occurred;
- every profile with empty exclusive inversion graph was `F2`-acyclic, agreeing with the homotopy proof.

### Additional tests

- **1,707** product-edge-link suspension identities were checked over `F2` for all comparable pairs in all naturally labelled coarse posets through five states;
- **3,000** deterministic random five-state profile trials were run; **639** nonempty matching cases were checked directly over `F2`, with **0 failures**;
- direct integral computations give `H_2=Z` for the Boolean endpoint `B_2` example and `H_3=Z` for `B_3`;
- the three-chain star counterexample gives actual `H_1=Z` while the false pairwise-link extension predicts zero.

A separate Horn verifier exhaustively checked all nonempty Boolean relations through four coordinates:

- dimension 4 contains **4,959** meet-closed relations and **4,959** join-closed relations;
- every meet-closed relation and its projection had a least element;
- every join-closed relation and its projection had a greatest element.

A distributive-lattice verifier checked all order-ideal lattices generated by naturally labelled posets through three generators (10 cases): the endpoint formula agreed exactly with direct integral computation, with the Boolean cases spherical and every non-Boolean distributive case neutral.

---

## 15. Comparison of the four requested programs

| Program | Outcome | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Boolean/Horn signature posets | Pure Horn/dual-Horn refined relations are exactly neutral; bounded/distributive matching gives a clean sphere-or-zero formula | **Exact, but the Horn part is topologically trivial; Boolean/distributive corollary is useful** |
| Bounded comparability | Height `<=2` remains completely classified by the prior rooted theorem; height 3 already allows torsion; coarse chains have a known Ferrers/independence-complex classification | **No new universal bounded-comparability classification** |
| Controlled lower/upper fibers | Classical fiber theorems give strong sufficient/decomposition results, but do not yield the new exact formula without added hypotheses | **Useful comparison, not the main result** |
| Descent / inversion filtration | Missing cores are bicliques of `G_psi`; the core-size filtration gives a spectral sequence; matching forces immediate collapse | **General mechanism + exact matching collapse** |

---

## 16. Literature and novelty boundary

The closest prior work found is not nerve theory but **simplicial vertex-deletion / obstruction-complex theory**.

1. Björner--Wachs--Welker, *Poset fiber theorems*, Trans. AMS 357 (2005), gives homotopy decompositions of a poset from lower fibers under connectivity assumptions.  This is the main benchmark for the controlled-fiber program.
2. Chachólski--Jin--Scolamiero--Tombari, *Homotopical decompositions of simplicial and Vietoris Rips complexes*, J. Applied and Computational Topology 5 (2021), studies induced subcomplexes obtained from vertex covers and measures failure by obstruction complexes.  Its one-, two-, and several-outside-point constructions are the closest antecedent to the missing-copy model.
3. Dey--Hirani--Krishnamoorthy, *Optimal Homologous Cycles, Total Unimodularity, and Linear Programming*, SIAM J. Comput. 40 (2011), gives the relevant topological characterization of TU boundary matrices.
4. Stong's finite-space reductions, Barmak's poset form of Quillen's Theorem A, and Fernández--Minian relation/mapping-cylinder methods are standard background for the closure and fiber arguments.
5. Horn model classes being closed under componentwise conjunction/intersection is classical Boolean-CSP / closure-system theory.
6. Crosscut/shellability theory for distributive and semidistributive lattices supplies the sphere-or-contractible behavior used in the lattice corollary.

### Conservative priority assessment

I did **not** locate the following exact statement in the searched literature:

> for a Boolean carrier split, if the 1-only-to-0-only comparison graph is a matching, the complete integral mapping-cone homology is the direct sum of two-degree-shifted reduced homologies of the corresponding coarse edge links.

However, this statement is built from standard vertex-deletion/cofiber ingredients, especially close to the obstruction-complex framework of Chachólski et al.  It should therefore be presented as a **specialized exact recognition theorem for the observation-refinement model**, not as a claim that link/cofiber decomposition itself is new.

A publication-priority claim should remain qualified until a specialist literature referee has checked whether the matching specialization occurs implicitly in the vertex-cover/deletion literature.

The 2026 search also found recent work on discrete homotopy/homology of finite posets, but not this two-colour carrier-splitting classification.

---

## 17. Adversarial specialist reviews

### Referee A -- finite-poset topology

**Attack:** "This is just Quillen/Björner--Wachs--Welker after rewriting the fibers."

**Finding:** not fully.  BWW supplies a powerful homotopy decomposition when lower fibers meet connectivity hypotheses.  The matching formula works integrally without those hypotheses and allows arbitrary torsion through coarse edge links.  The proof, however, uses standard poset/order-complex ideas.  **Revision:** claim exact specialization, not foundational new fiber theory.

### Referee B -- combinatorial topology

**Attack:** "The missing-copy proof is generic vertex deletion."

**Finding:** substantially correct as a priority warning.  Chachólski et al. explicitly develop obstruction complexes and cofiber sequences for one, two, and several outside vertices.  **Revision:** position the new content in the observation-theoretic identification of missing copies, the exclusive inversion graph, the biclique filtration, and the matching direct-sum reduction.

### Referee C -- integer homology / TU

**Attack:** "Matching should force torsion-free or TU matrices."

**Finding:** false.  The endpoint construction transfers arbitrary reduced integral homology of a coarse link two degrees upward, including torsion.  **Revision:** remove any blanket TU suggestion and retain only the exact homology formula.

### Referee D -- Horn / closure systems

**Attack:** "Horn might give the desired nontrivial class."

**Finding:** when the whole refined relation is meet-closed, both refined and projected posets have minima and are contractible.  Pure Horn closure therefore trivializes the topological defect rather than classifying a rich one.  **Revision:** retain Horn as a neutral regime and use Boolean/distributive lattices as the nontrivial structured example.

### Hostile referee -- smallest destroyer

**Task:** destroy the edgewise formula as soon as matching is relaxed.

**Result:** the three-state chain with profile `(1-only, 0-only, 0-only)` does so.  The exclusive inversion graph is a forest, but the two inversion edges interact through a 2-simplex and produce `H_1=Z` even though the individual coarse edge links contribute zero.

This is a strong reason to keep the matching hypothesis explicit.

---

## 18. Success level

### **LEVEL A -- STRONG SUCCESS**

The rubric for Level A is met mathematically:

- the class is natural: noninteracting exclusive inversions;
- the classification is necessary-and-sufficient for all integral cone homology on that class;
- the theorem is all-dimensional;
- the proof is exact;
- exhaustive integral and targeted higher-order computation support it;
- a minimal failure outside the hypothesis is known.

The **priority confidence is lower than the correctness confidence** because general obstruction-complex/vertex-deletion theory is close prior art.  The paper should distinguish those two judgments.

---

## 19. Answers to the ten required questions

1. **Does a nontrivial higher-dimensional exact classification exist?**  **Yes.**  Exclusive-inversion matching gives an exact all-dimensional integral formula.
2. **Strongest class?**  Carrier-splitting systems for which the bipartite graph of `1`-only-to-`0`-only coarse comparisons is a matching.
3. **Exact theorem?**  Formula (5.2): the cone homology is the direct sum of two-degree-shifted reduced homologies of the corresponding coarse edge links.
4. **Integral, field-dependent, or rational?**  **Integral.**  It holds over arbitrary coefficients.
5. **Does torsion occur?**  **Yes.**  Arbitrary finite-poset link torsion can be transferred two degrees upward.
6. **Stronger than standard poset-fiber theory?**  **As a specialized computation, yes:** it gives exact groups without BWW connectivity hypotheses.  **As general topology, no:** its proof sits close to standard vertex-deletion/cofiber machinery.
7. **Does it recover the `h_psi(Q)<=2` rooted-forest theorem?**  On the matching locus, yes at the homology level.  The general interaction-core filtration specializes to the deleted-edge/deleted-triangle incidence complex underlying the full low-height theorem.  The matching theorem by itself does not subsume every low-height nonmatching case.
8. **Smallest counterexample outside the hypothesis?**  Three-chain `0<1<2` with profile `(1,0,0)`; exclusive graph `K_{1,2}`, actual `H_1=Z`, naive edge-link sum zero.
9. **Should it replace the carrier-splitting theorem as the paper's main result?**  **Not replace; strengthen.**  The carrier-splitting factorization is the general structural theorem.  The matching-link theorem should become the strongest exact all-height theorem immediately after it.
10. **Single next theorem?**  Construct and classify the **exclusive-inversion interaction spectral sequence** beyond matching, beginning with exclusive graphs of maximum degree two or chordal/Ferrers biclique structure, and determine conditions forcing collapse at `E^2`.

---

## 20. Recommended manuscript action

The result is strong enough to justify a new manuscript section, but not a wholesale rewrite of the paper yet.

Insert, in this order:

1. the full-doubling / missing-copy model;
2. the two-colour deletion square and shift isomorphism;
3. the exclusive inversion graph;
4. the interaction-core filtration;
5. the matching-link theorem and proof;
6. bounded-poset and Boolean/distributive corollaries;
7. the three-chain forest counterexample;
8. the torsion/universality sharpness result;
9. a literature paragraph explicitly crediting obstruction-complex deletion theory.

The next gate should attack degree-two interaction rather than broadening the theorem by wishful analogy from matching to forests.
