\section{All-height carrier splitting under noninteracting exclusive inversions}
\label{sec:exclusive-matching}

The low-height rooted-incidence theorem gives a complete answer when the
weighted height is at most two.  In higher dimensions a universal rooted-forest
criterion is impossible: the same-carrier boundary case already supports
integral torsion and arbitrary finite-poset homotopy types.  Nevertheless, an
all-height exact classification survives when the genuinely incompatible
carrier outcomes do not interact.

Let
\[
A_a=\{s\in Q:(s,a)\in Q^\psi\},\qquad a\in\{0,1\},
\]
and put
\[
P=A_1\setminus A_0,\qquad Z=A_0\setminus A_1,\qquad
C=A_0\cap A_1.
\]
Thus $P$ consists of the $1$-only coarse states, $Z$ of the $0$-only coarse
states, and $C$ of the states that genuinely split.

\begin{definition}[Exclusive inversion graph]
\label{def:exclusive-inversion-graph}
The \emph{exclusive inversion graph} is the bipartite graph
\[
G_\psi=(P\sqcup Z,E_\psi),\qquad
E_\psi=\{(p,z)\in P\times Z:p<z\text{ in }Q\}.
\]
An edge records a coarse comparison whose earlier endpoint admits only the new
outcome $1$ while its later endpoint admits only $0$.
\end{definition}

\subsection{The full-doubling model}

Let
\[
D=Q\times\{0<1\},\qquad K=\Delta D,\qquad L=\Delta Q^\psi.
\]
The actual refined carrier is the induced subposet of $D$ obtained by deleting
exactly
\[
M_0=\{(p,0):p\in P\},\qquad
M_1=\{(z,1):z\in Z\}.
\]
Let $K_P$ be obtained by deleting $M_0$, let $K_Z$ be obtained by deleting
$M_1$, and put
\[
U=K_P\cup K_Z,\qquad L=K_P\cap K_Z.
\]
The complex $K_P$ closes upward to the full top row, while $K_Z$ closes
downward to the full bottom row.  Hence both $K_P\hookrightarrow K$ and
$K_Z\hookrightarrow K$ are homotopy equivalences.  The long exact sequences
of triples together with simplicial excision give
\begin{equation}
H_n(K,L;R)\cong H_{n+1}(K,U;R)
\label{eq:two-colour-shift}
\end{equation}
for every coefficient ring $R$.  Since $D\to Q$ is a homotopy equivalence,
$H_n(K,L;R)$ is the reduced homology of the homotopy cofiber of the refined
projection $\Delta\pi:\Delta Q^\psi\to\Delta Q$.

A simplex of $K\setminus U$ contains at least one missing lower copy $(p,0)$
and at least one missing upper copy $(z,1)$.  Because it is a product-order
chain, every such pair satisfies $p<z$.  Therefore the missing vertices of a
relative simplex project to a complete bipartite subgraph of $G_\psi$.  This
observation isolates the source of higher interaction: bicliques with more than
one edge couple otherwise local defects.

\begin{theorem}[Exclusive-Inversion Matching Theorem]
\label{thm:exclusive-matching}
Suppose that the exclusive inversion graph $G_\psi$ is a matching.  Then, for
every coefficient ring $R$ and every integer $n$,
\begin{equation}
\widetilde H_n\!\left(\Cone(\Delta\pi);R\right)
\cong
\bigoplus_{(p,z)\in E_\psi}
\widetilde H_{n-2}\!\left(
\operatorname{lk}_{\Delta Q}[p,z];R
\right).
\label{eq:exclusive-matching}
\end{equation}
Consequently $\Delta\pi$ is an $R$-homology equivalence if and only if every
coarse edge link $\operatorname{lk}_{\Delta Q}[p,z]$ indexed by an exclusive
inversion is $R$-acyclic.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A relative simplex of $(K,U)$ contains at least one vertex of $M_0$ and one
vertex of $M_1$.  If it contained two missing lower vertices and one missing
upper vertex, the corresponding upper endpoint would have degree at least two
in $G_\psi$; the dual statement holds for two missing upper vertices.  The
matching hypothesis therefore forces every relative simplex to contain a unique
mixed pair
\[
e=((p,0)<(z,1)),\qquad (p,z)\in E_\psi.
\]
Deleting either endpoint of $e$ sends the simplex into $U$, while deleting any
other vertex preserves the same pair.  Hence the relative chain complex splits
as
\[
C_m(K,U;R)=\bigoplus_{e\in E_\psi}C_m^{(e)},
\qquad
C_m^{(e)}\cong
\widetilde C_{m-2}(\operatorname{lk}_K e;R).
\]
Thus
\[
H_m(K,U;R)\cong
\bigoplus_{e\in E_\psi}
\widetilde H_{m-2}(\operatorname{lk}_K e;R).
\]

It remains to identify the product-order link.  For
$e=((p,0)<(z,1))$, its link factors into the lower interval, the open middle
interval, and the upper interval.  The open middle interval is covered by two
contractible subposets: delete $(z,0)$ and close upward to the bit-$1$ row, or
delete $(p,1)$ and close downward to the bit-$0$ row.  Their intersection is
$(p,z)_Q\times\{0<1\}$, homotopy equivalent to $(p,z)_Q$.  Since $(p,1)$ and
$(z,0)$ are incomparable, every middle-chain lies in one of these two pieces;
therefore
\[
\Delta((p,0),(z,1))\simeq\Sigma\Delta(p,z)_Q.
\]
Joining with the lower and upper factors gives
\[
\operatorname{lk}_{\Delta(Q\times\mathbf2)}e
\simeq
\Sigma\operatorname{lk}_{\Delta Q}[p,z].
\]
Combining this suspension shift with~\eqref{eq:two-colour-shift} yields
\eqref{eq:exclusive-matching}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Bounded-poset localization]
\label{cor:bounded-localization}
Assume that $Q$ has a global minimum $\hat0$ and maximum $\hat1$, and that
$G_\psi$ is a matching.  Then every exclusive edge except possibly
$(\hat0,\hat1)$ has contractible coarse edge link.  Hence only the global
endpoint inversion can contribute to the cone homology.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
If $p\ne\hat0$, the lower factor $\Delta Q_{<p}$ has the minimum $\hat0$; if
$z\ne\hat1$, the upper factor $\Delta Q_{>z}$ has the maximum $\hat1$.  In
either case the edge link is a join with a nonempty contractible complex.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Distributive endpoint profile]
\label{cor:distributive-endpoint}
Let $Q=J(R)$ be the lattice of order ideals of a finite poset $R$.  Make the
bottom state $1$-only, the top state $0$-only, and every other state split.  If
$R$ is an $r$-element antichain, so that $Q=B_r$, then
\[
\widetilde H_r(\Cone(\Delta\pi);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z
\]
and all other reduced cone homology vanishes.  If $R$ is not an antichain,
the cone is integrally acyclic.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Corollary~\ref{cor:bounded-localization} reduces the answer to the reduced
homology of the proper part of $J(R)$, shifted by two.  The atom crosscut is a
full simplex unless the atoms join to the top element.  In $J(R)$ the atoms
correspond to the minimal elements of $R$, and they join to the top exactly
when every element of $R$ is minimal, i.e. exactly when $R$ is an antichain.
In that case $J(R)=B_r$ and its proper part is homotopy equivalent to
$S^{r-2}$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Sharpness: interaction begins at the first shared endpoint}

The matching condition cannot be weakened merely to ``$G_\psi$ is a
forest.''  For the three-element chain $0<1<2$ with availability profile
\[
0:\{1\},\qquad 1:\{0\},\qquad 2:\{0\},
\]
the exclusive graph is the two-edge star $K_{1,2}$.  Direct integral Smith
normal form gives
\[
\widetilde H_1(\Cone(\Delta\pi);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z,
\]
while the sum of the two individual coarse-edge-link contributions is zero.
The shared endpoint creates a three-vertex interaction core and a differential
between the two edge defects.

Nor does matching imply total unimodularity or torsion-freeness.  Given any
nonempty finite poset $R$, take
\[
Q=\hat0\oplus R\oplus\hat1
\]
and use the endpoint profile above.  There is exactly one exclusive inversion,
and Theorem~\ref{thm:exclusive-matching} gives
\[
\widetilde H_n(\Cone(\Delta\pi);\mathbb Z)
\cong
\widetilde H_{n-2}(\Delta R;\mathbb Z).
\]
Thus arbitrary finite-poset homology, including torsion, can occur even inside
the matching class.  In particular, total unimodularity must be controlled by
stronger conditions on the relevant links; global torsion-freeness alone is
not a TU criterion~\cite{DeyHiraniKrishnamoorthy2011}.

\subsection{Beyond matching: the interaction-core filtration}

For a relative simplex $\sigma\in K\setminus U$, define its missing core
\[
S(\sigma)=\sigma\cap(M_0\cup M_1).
\]
Filter $C_*(K,U)$ by $|S(\sigma)|$.  If $\mathcal C_r$ is the family of mixed
$r$-vertex missing cores that are simplices of $K$ and
\[
\Lambda_S=\operatorname{lk}_K(S)[V(L)],
\]
then the associated graded complex is
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{gr}_r C_m(K,U)
\cong
\bigoplus_{S\in\mathcal C_r}
\widetilde C_{m-r}(\Lambda_S).
\label{eq:interaction-graded}
\end{equation}
Indeed, deleting an available vertex preserves $S$, while deleting a missing
vertex lowers the filtration.  This produces a convergent interaction spectral
sequence whose first page is assembled from the homology of the
$\Lambda_S$.  The cores project to chain-supported bicliques of $G_\psi$.
Under the matching hypothesis only $r=2$ occurs, so the spectral sequence
collapses immediately and recovers Theorem~\ref{thm:exclusive-matching}.

This filtration is the natural next object beyond matching.  The smallest
nonmatching example above shows that shared endpoints already create higher
core differentials; therefore a higher-dimensional analogue of the low-height
rooted-forest theorem must control these interactions rather than only the
acyclicity of $G_\psi$.

\begin{remark}[Priority boundary]
The deletion/cofiber technology used here is classical.  In particular,
vertex-cover obstruction complexes already provide general homotopical tools
for comparing a complex with unions of induced subcomplexes
\cite{ChacholskiEtAl2021}, while poset-fiber decompositions give broad results
under fiber-connectivity hypotheses \cite{BjornerWachsWelker2005}.  The
candidate contribution of Theorem~\ref{thm:exclusive-matching} is the
observation-theoretic two-colour recognition and the resulting exact coarse
edge-link formula.  No claim is made that simplicial vertex deletion or
homotopy cofibers themselves are new.
\end{remark}

\section{Carrier splitting under a new Boolean observation}\label{sec:carrier-splitting}

We now treat the refinement regime left open in the previous draft: a new
observation is not constant on every current observational-equivalence class, so
one old $T_0$ state can split into two refined states.  This operation is not a
cover refinement and is not, on its face, a same-carrier order thinning.  It does,
however, admit a canonical factorization through one.

Let $W$ be the finite world set, let $\Phi$ be the current observation family,
and write
\[
 Q=o_\Phi(W)\subseteq\{0,1\}^{I}
\]
for the finite $T_0$ quotient ordered coordinatewise.  Add one Boolean
observation $\psi$.  The refined quotient is
\[
 Q^\psi=o_{\Phi\cup\{\psi\}}(W)
 \subseteq Q\times\{0,1\},
\]
with the product order.  Let
\[
 \pi:Q^\psi\longrightarrow Q,
 \qquad \pi(s,a)=s,
\]
be the coordinate-forgetting map.  For $a\in\{0,1\}$ put
\[
 A_a:=\{s\in Q:(s,a)\in Q^\psi\},
 \qquad C:=A_0\cap A_1.
\]
Thus $A_0\cup A_1=Q$, and $C$ is precisely the set of old observational
states that split.

\begin{definition}[Split completion]
On the same carrier as $Q^\psi$, define the split-completion order
$\widehat Q^\psi$ by
\[
 (s,a)\leq_{\widehat Q}(t,b)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \bigl(s<t\text{ in }Q\bigr)
 \ \text{or}\ 
 \bigl(s=t\text{ and }a\leq b\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, $\widehat Q^\psi$ is the lexicographic sum over $Q$ of the
nonempty fiber chains
\[
 F_s:=\{a\in\{0,1\}:(s,a)\in Q^\psi\}.
\]
Let $b(s,a)=a$ be the new-bit label on this expanded carrier.
\end{definition}

The distinction between $Q^\psi$ and $\widehat Q^\psi$ is exact.  The split
completion remembers every old comparison between coarse states, independently
of the new bit.  The actual refined order keeps only those comparisons along
which the new bit is nondecreasing.

\begin{theorem}[Carrier-splitting factorization]\label{thm:split-factorization}
With the notation above:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item the projection $p:\widehat Q^\psi\to Q$, $p(s,a)=s$, is a homotopy
  equivalence of finite posets; in fact $\widehat Q^\psi$ beat-reduces to a
  subposet isomorphic to $Q$;
\item the actual refined quotient is exactly the one-bit thinning of the split
  completion,
  \[
    Q^\psi=(\widehat Q^\psi)_b,
  \]
  meaning that a comparison $x<_{\widehat Q}y$ is retained precisely when
  $b(x)\leq b(y)$;
\item if $i:\Delta(Q^\psi)\hookrightarrow\Delta(\widehat Q^\psi)$ is the
  inclusion, then $\Delta(\pi)=\Delta(p)\circ i$, and there is a homotopy
  equivalence of homotopy cofibers
  \[
  \operatorname{Cof}(\Delta\pi)\simeq
  \operatorname{Cof}(i).
  \]
  Consequently, for every coefficient ring $R$,
  \[
  \widetilde H_n\!\left(\Cone(\Delta\pi);R\right)
  \cong
  H_n\!\left(\Delta(\widehat Q^\psi),\Delta(Q^\psi);R\right).
  \]
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For every split state $s\in C$, the lower copy $(s,0)$ is an up-beat point of
$\widehat Q^\psi$: its strict upper set has the minimum $(s,1)$, because
$(s,1)$ lies below every copy over every $t>s$.  Remove these lower split
copies one at a time.  What remains has one representative over each $s\in Q$
and is order-isomorphic to $Q$.  Beat-point removal is a strong deformation
retraction for finite $T_0$ spaces, giving (i).

For distinct coarse states $s<t$, the split completion always contains
$(s,a)<(t,b)$ whenever those copies exist.  The product order on $Q^\psi$
retains exactly the cases $a\leq b$.  The same statement holds within a split
fiber, where $(s,0)<(s,1)$ is retained.  This proves (ii).  Part (iii) follows
from $\pi=p\circ i$ and homotopy invariance of the homotopy cofiber under
postcomposition by the homotopy equivalence $\Delta(p)$.  Since $i$ is a
simplicial inclusion, its homotopy cofiber computes the relative homology of
its simplicial pair.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What is standard and what is specific]
Beat-point reduction is classical finite-space topology, and homotopy cofiber
invariance is standard.  The project-specific content is the observation-theoretic
factorization: an actual split of $T_0$ observational states is converted canonically
into a homotopy-neutral lexicographic expansion followed by the precise one-bit
monotonicity thinning already studied on a fixed carrier.  Thus carrier splitting
is not a fourth unrelated operation; it is a neutral blow-up plus an order defect.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The exact inversion-chain complex}

Theorem~\ref{thm:split-factorization} gives a chain-level classification without
any nerve hypothesis.

\begin{theorem}[Inversion-chain model]\label{thm:inversion-chain}
For any coefficient ring $R$, the relative group
\[
 C_k\!\left(\Delta(\widehat Q^\psi),\Delta(Q^\psi);R\right)
\]
is free on the strict chains
\[
 x_0<_{\widehat Q}x_1<_{\widehat Q}\cdots<_{\widehat Q}x_k
\]
whose bit word
\[
 b(x_0)b(x_1)\cdots b(x_k)
\]
is not weakly increasing.  Equivalently, a relative generator is exactly a
split-completion chain containing an inversion $1\cdots0$.  Its relative boundary
is the ordinary alternating simplicial boundary with every monotone-bit face set
to zero.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The two order complexes have the same vertex set.  A split-completion chain is a
simplex of $\Delta(Q^\psi)$ exactly when every comparison in the chain survives
the one-bit thinning, which is equivalent to the bit word being weakly increasing.
Quotienting the simplicial chain groups therefore leaves exactly the nonmonotone
chains, and the relative differential is the induced simplicial differential.
\end{proof}

This formulation is useful computationally: the defect depends only on the old
signature poset and the three-valued fiber profile
\[
 F_s\in\bigl\{\{0\},\{1\},\{0,1\}\bigr\},
\]
not on the number of worlds inside each old equivalence class.

\subsection{Immediate homotopy-neutrality criteria}

The factorization also reveals when splitting is automatically conservative.

\begin{proposition}[Monotone-section criterion]\label{prop:monotone-section}
If $A_1$ is an upward-closed subset of $Q$, then $\pi:Q^\psi\to Q$ is a
homotopy equivalence.  Dually, if $A_0$ is downward closed, then $\pi$ is a
homotopy equivalence.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Assume $A_1$ is upward closed.  Define
\[
 r_+(s)=
 \begin{cases}
 (s,1),&s\in A_1,\\
 (s,0),&s\notin A_1.
 \end{cases}
\]
The upset condition makes $r_+$ order preserving, and $\pi r_+=\mathrm{id}_Q$.
Moreover every $(s,a)\in Q^\psi$ satisfies $(s,a)\leq r_+(s)$, so
$\mathrm{id}_{Q^\psi}\leq r_+\pi$.  The order-homotopy lemma gives
$r_+\pi\simeq\mathrm{id}$ and hence $\pi$ is a homotopy equivalence.  The
$A_0$ statement is dual, using the minimum available bit in each fiber.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Common-outcome anchor]
If every old observational state has at least one refined world with $\psi=1$
($A_1=Q$), or every old state has at least one with $\psi=0$ ($A_0=Q$), then
carrier splitting is homotopy-neutral.  In particular, if every old state genuinely
splits, so $A_0=A_1=Q$, then $Q^\psi=Q\times\{0<1\}$ and the projection is a
homotopy equivalence.
\end{corollary}

Thus the act of duplicating a state is not itself the source of topological defect.
The defect is caused by incompatible outcome availability across comparable coarse
states: a lower state that can realize $1$ together with an upper state that can
realize $0$ creates a potentially deleted comparison.

\subsection{Localization by lower fibers}

For $s\in Q$ define the lower fiber
\[
 L_s:=\pi^{-1}(Q_{\leq s}).
\]
If $s\in A_1$, then $(s,1)$ is a maximum of $L_s$, hence $L_s$ is
contractible.  Therefore all lower-fiber obstructions to Quillen-type equivalence
localize to the $0$-only states $A_0\setminus A_1$.  Dually, all upper-fiber
obstructions localize to the $1$-only states $A_1\setminus A_0$.

This observation does not replace the exact relative complex above.  It does,
however, connect the carrier-splitting problem to the classical poset-fiber
framework.  Under the connectivity hypotheses of the Bj\"orner--Wachs--Welker
fiber theorem, the source $\Delta(Q^\psi)$ admits a wedge decomposition in terms
of the noncontractible lower fibers and upper links.  The important point here is
that the split fibers themselves disappear from that list whenever their top copy
is present.

\subsection{Exact low-height classification}

The general inversion complex can have arbitrarily high dimension.  In the first
nontrivial dimensional regime it collapses to graph incidence and admits a closed
integral classification.

\begin{definition}[Weighted split height]
Let $C=A_0\cap A_1$ be the split set.  Define
\[
 h_\psi(Q)
 :=\max_{s_0<\cdots<s_r\text{ in }Q}
 \left(r+\#\{j:s_j\in C\}\right).
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:split-height}
$h_\psi(Q)=\dim\Delta(\widehat Q^\psi)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A strict coarse chain contributes one vertex from every fiber, and a split fiber can
contribute both copies consecutively.  Taking both copies at every split state on the
chain attains the displayed number, and no split-completion chain can contain more.
\end{proof}

Suppose $h_\psi(Q)\leq2$.  An \emph{inversion edge} is a deleted order-complex edge
of $\Delta(\widehat Q^\psi)$, equivalently a pair
\[
 (s,1)<_{\widehat Q}(t,0),\qquad s<t,
\]
with $s\in A_1$ and $t\in A_0$.  A deleted triangle has one of the four nonmonotone
bit patterns
\[
 010,\qquad100,\qquad101,\qquad110.
\]
It therefore contains either one or two inversion edges.  Introduce one formal root
for each connected component of $Q$ (equivalently of $\widehat Q^\psi$).  The
\emph{carrier-split defect graph} $G_\psi(Q)$ has one vertex for every inversion edge;
a deleted triangle with two inversion edges joins their vertices, while a deleted
triangle with one inversion edge joins that vertex to the root of its component.
Parallel graph edges are allowed.

\begin{theorem}[Carrier-splitting cone classification in weighted height two]
\label{thm:carrier-graph}
Assume $h_\psi(Q)\leq2$.  Let $c_0(G_\psi)$ be the number of connected components
of $G_\psi(Q)$ containing no formal root.  Then
\[
 \widetilde H_n\!\left(\Cone(\Delta\pi);\mathbb Z\right)
 \cong
 \begin{cases}
   \mathbb Z^{\beta_1(G_\psi)},&n=2,\\
   \mathbb Z^{c_0(G_\psi)},&n=1,\\
   0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
The relative boundary matrix is totally unimodular.  Hence the same Betti ranks hold
over every field.  Moreover the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item the carrier-splitting cone is acyclic over $\mathbb Z$;
\item it is acyclic over every field;
\item $G_\psi(Q)$ is a rooted forest;
\item $\Delta(\widehat Q^\psi)$ collapses onto $\Delta(Q^\psi)$ through deleted
edge--triangle pairs;
\item $\Delta\pi:\Delta(Q^\psi)\to\Delta(Q)$ is a homotopy equivalence.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:split-factorization}, the mapping-cone homology is the relative
homology of the one-bit thinning
$\Delta(Q^\psi)\subseteq\Delta(\widehat Q^\psi)$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:split-height}
places the split completion in dimension at most two.  The one-bit height-two
incidence theorem from the companion order-thinning analysis applies verbatim: the
relative $C_2\to C_1$ boundary is the oriented incidence matrix of the rooted defect
graph with root rows deleted.  Ordinary graph incidence gives the two displayed free
homology groups and total unimodularity; the rooted-forest condition is equivalent to
perfect relative cancellation and to an elementary collapse.  Finally
$\Delta(p)$ is already a homotopy equivalence, so two-out-of-three identifies
homotopy neutrality of the inclusion with homotopy neutrality of $\Delta\pi$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Status of the low-height theorem]
The graph-incidence algebra, total unimodularity, rooted forests, and beat-point
technology are standard.  The exact height-two theorem for one-bit thinning is proved
in the companion structural-computation manuscript.  The new point here is the
carrier-splitting reduction that makes that theorem applicable to a process which
changes the $T_0$ carrier.  Accordingly, this theorem should be positioned as an
exact transfer theorem, not as a new general theory of rooted forests.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Sharpness beyond weighted height two}

No coefficient-independent forest criterion can hold in unrestricted dimension.
The carrier-splitting family contains the no-split case $C=\varnothing$, which is
exactly arbitrary same-carrier one-bit thinning.  Companion results show that one-bit
thinning in height three can already have relative integral torsion, and in unrestricted
height can encode arbitrary finite-poset homotopy types inside a contractible coarse
cone.  If one insists that at least one old state genuinely split, a disjoint neutral
split component may be adjoined without changing positive-degree cone homology.
Thus the weighted-height-two hypothesis in Theorem~\ref{thm:carrier-graph} marks a
real boundary rather than a presentational convenience.

The appropriate all-height object is therefore the inversion-chain complex of
Theorem~\ref{thm:inversion-chain}, supplemented where useful by poset-fiber or
homotopy-colimit methods.  A realistic next target is not another universal forest
theorem, but a classification of higher-dimensional inversion complexes under
additional structural hypotheses on $Q$ and on the split profile $(A_0,A_1)$.

# Literature and Priority Map — Gluing Concepts

## Scope and method

This search was organized by **mathematical structure**, not by the phrase “mental space.” It covered simplicial/categorical gluing, join decomposition, sheaf/cosheaf local-to-global methods, Boolean and relational factorization, Formal Concept Analysis, formal conceptual blending, conceptual spaces, contextuality, and current work through September 2026.

The priority conclusion is conservative: the project contains a useful modern synthesis and one clean cross-layer factorization lemma, but the broad ingredients all have substantial antecedents. No claim that “concepts can be glued” or “concepts can be decomposed” is currently defensible as a new theorem by itself.

## Closest antecedents

| Area | Source | Exact overlap with this project | Priority consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Simplicial pushouts/colimits | Standard category of simplicial complexes; e.g. Clara Löh, *Applied Algebraic Topology* lecture notes | Common-face gluing is a categorical colimit; under literal inclusions it is the union after identifying the overlap. | Ordinary simplicial gluing is standard. |
| Mayer–Vietoris | Allen Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology* (2002), Ch. 2 | The short exact chain sequence and resulting long exact Mayer–Vietoris sequence are the standard chain-level account of a union. | Chain-level “interaction of overlap” is useful but not novel. |
| Nerve theorem | Standard nerve theorem; e.g. Chazal–de Silva–Glisse–Oudot course material | A good cover is recoverable up to homotopy from its intersection nerve. | Nerve is an assembly invariant, but not a full semantic reconstruction mechanism. |
| Sheaf gluing | Stacks Project, Tag 006S (current) | Sections agreeing on pairwise overlaps glue uniquely in a sheaf. | The thesis's later “compatible sections” idea has a direct standard formalization. |
| Cosheaves | Justin Curry, *Sheaves, Cosheaves and Applications* (2013), arXiv:1303.3255 | Covariant local-to-global aggregation on cell complexes. | Cosheaf aggregation is a natural tool, not a new construction. |
| Conceptual blending by colimits/pushouts | Bou, Plaza & Schorlemmer, “Amalgams, Colimits, and Conceptual Blending,” in *Concept Invention* (2018); Schorlemmer & Plaza (2021) | Conceptual blending is formalized representation-independently with category-theoretic amalgams/colimits; the 2021 paper proves essential equivalence to Goguen's pushout model in an ordered category of partial maps. | This is the closest direct priority barrier to a broad “gluing concepts by pushout” claim. |
| Formal governing principles for blends | Bourou et al., “Characterising cognitively useful blends” (2024) | Continues the category-theoretic blending program and formalizes integration/topology-preservation principles. | The literature is active and already asks when a blend is structurally appropriate. |
| Sheaf semantic compositionality | Steven Phillips, “Sheaving—a universal construction for semantic compositionality” (2020) | Uses sheafification/local-to-global coherence as a model of semantic compositionality. | Very close to using sheaves to glue local concept information into a coherent whole. |
| Join decomposition of complexes | Kevin Marshall & Jeremy L. Martin, “Hopf monoids of set families,” *Australasian Journal of Combinatorics* 92(3) (2025), 419–449 | For simplicial complexes the product is join; the paper identifies a unique finest join representation via its support-system/fundamental-inflator formalism. | A canonical finest join decomposition is already explicit in current literature. |
| Stanley–Reisner/join factorization | Amelotte & Briggs, “Product decompositions of moment-angle manifolds and B-rigidity” (2023) | Shows a nontrivial tensor-product decomposition of relevant Koszul homology iff the simplicial complex decomposes as a join of full subcomplexes, in its Gorenstein setting. | Algebraic detection of joins has strong prior art. |
| Boolean function decomposition | Ashenhurst, Curtis, Karp; survey: Jan C. Bioch, “Decomposition of Boolean Functions” | Classical variable-partition/function-composition theory for Boolean functions. | General Boolean “disentanglement” is long-established; CM claims must be narrower. |
| Finite relational factorization | Olteanu, Koch & Antova, “World-set decompositions” (2008; ICDT 2007 precursor) | Relational product decomposition, polynomial factorization, and a unique maximal decomposition for WSD relations. | Cartesian semantic factorization and prime factors are established tools. |
| Formal Concept Analysis | Ganter & Wille, *Formal Concept Analysis: Mathematical Foundations*, 2nd ed. (2024) | Entire chapters on “Parts, factors, and bonds” and “Decompositions of concept lattices.” | “Concept factor/decomposition” already has a mature mathematical literature. |
| FCA independent subcontexts | Aragón, Medina-Moreno & Ramírez-Poussa (2025) | Defines independent subcontexts and relates their decompositions to independent blocks of concept lattices. | Especially close to the project's independence/disentanglement vocabulary. |

## Priority assessment by proposed contribution

### A. “A concept can be glued by a pushout/colimit”
**Priority status: blocked.** This is standard category theory and has been applied directly to conceptual blending.

### B. “Compatible local concept data can be glued by sheaves”
**Priority status: blocked as a broad claim.** The sheaf axiom is standard, and Phillips explicitly used sheafification for semantic compositionality.

### C. “A simplicial complex has a finest join factorization”
**Priority status: blocked as a broad claim.** Current join-decomposition literature already contains a unique-finest representation, and the minimal-nonface criterion used here is an elementary reformulation.

### D. “Boolean/relational concept semantics can be factorized”
**Priority status: blocked as a broad claim.** Boolean functional decomposition and finite relational product factorization are established.

### E. “A structured concept should require the *same partition* to factor both its simplicial carrier and its semantic layer”
**Priority status: plausible synthesis, not yet demonstrated as theorem-level novelty.** The least-common-coarsening theorem in this audit follows quickly once the two prime decompositions are available. I found no source in this search that packages exactly the simplicial-join and semantic-product factors together as a ‘concept’ invariant, but the ingredients are standard enough that this alone should not be advertised as a major new theorem without a dedicated priority search.

### F. “Succinct structured factorization for a compact complex plus Boolean/CM semantics”
**Priority status: promising open direction.** This is where the project may become technically distinctive: avoid explicit truth-table expansion, exploit structural decomposition as a speedup, classify complexity, and prove canonical factorization results for meaningful succinct classes.

## What is defensibly distinctive now?

The strongest defensible contribution is a **disciplined synthesis** that separates four notions that the thesis blended together:

1. non-completing simplicial gluing;
2. completion/filling of a higher simplex;
3. local-to-global semantic coherence;
4. independent-factor decomposition.

The synthesis then forces structural and semantic decompositions to use the same attribute partition. That is a useful research architecture, but the literature search does **not** yet justify a strong novelty claim.

# Formal Gluing Definitions

## 1. Recommended ontology

The 2015 thesis alternates between calling a concept a simplex-like unit and defining a concept as a connected simplicial complex. The cleanest modern repair is **not** to choose one and erase the other, but to separate levels.

**Atomic concept.** An atomic concept is a nonempty finite **labelled simplex**
\[
\sigma=\Delta(V_\sigma)=\{\tau:\tau\subseteq V_\sigma\},
\]
whose vertices carry declared semantic labels (attributes, predicates, variables, or other primitive features). The simplex asserts that the listed vertices participate jointly in one atomic conceptual episode/object. This is a modeling convention, not a psychological fact.

**Concept complex.** A conceptual/mental structure is a finite abstract simplicial complex \(K\). Its maximal simplices are atomic concepts; intersections encode shared sub-concepts/incidence. This retains the thesis's useful idea that concepts can themselves be assembled into a larger simplicial structure.

**Structured concept.** For nontrivial gluing and independence, the topological carrier should be enriched. The minimal useful schema is
\[
\mathcal C=(K,\lambda,\mathcal S),
\]
where \(K\) is a finite simplicial complex, \(\lambda\) is label/provenance data, and \(\mathcal S\) is an optional semantic layer (a Boolean relation/function, CM/LM truth tensor, presheaf/sheaf, or other constraint system). No theorem should depend on a semantic layer that has not been explicitly declared.

This is option 3 in the prompt: **a simplex as an atomic concept and a complex as a mental/conceptual structure**, with additional structure when the question is semantic rather than merely combinatorial.

## 2. Basic simplicial objects

An abstract simplicial complex on vertex set \(V\) is a downward-closed family \(K\subseteq 2^V\) containing \(\varnothing\). A simplex on \(S\subseteq V\) is \(\Delta(S)=2^S\). A subcomplex \(L\subseteq K\) is a downward-closed subfamily. The induced/full subcomplex on \(A\subseteq V\) is
\[
K|_A=\{\sigma\in K:\sigma\subseteq A\}.
\]

For two subcomplexes \(A,B\subseteq K\), their set-theoretic union and intersection are again subcomplexes. In particular, if \(K=A\cup B\), then \(A\cap B\) is the natural overlap object.

## 3. Default gluing: pushout along a specified overlap

Let
\[
D\xrightarrow{i}A,\qquad D\xrightarrow{j}B
\]
be simplicial embeddings. The **simplicial pushout** \(A\cup_D B\) is the categorical colimit of this span. When the maps are literal subcomplex inclusions, it is the ordinary union after identifying the common copy of \(D\).

The important property is negative as well as positive:

> **No-completion property.** A simplex is present in the pushout only because it came from \(A\) or \(B\) (after vertex identifications). The pushout does not invent cross-simplices whose vertices came from both sides.

This is exactly why two edges \(ab\) and \(bc\) glued at \(b\) form a path rather than a filled triangle, and why four triangular faces of a tetrahedron form its boundary rather than its 3-simplex interior.

### 3.1 When is a union of two simplices itself a simplex?

Let \(A=\Delta(S)\) and \(B=\Delta(T)\) be simplices and take the ordinary simplicial union. Then
\[
A\cup B\text{ is a simplex}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S\subseteq T\text{ or }T\subseteq S.
\]

**Proof.** If one vertex set contains the other, the union is the larger simplex. Conversely, if neither contains the other, choose \(s\in S\setminus T\) and \(t\in T\setminus S\). A simplex on \(S\cup T\) would contain the edge \(\{s,t\}\), but that edge is in neither \(A\) nor \(B\), so it is absent from the union. ∎

Thus ordinary gluing of genuinely different concepts almost always yields a **general complex**, not one larger simplex.

## 4. Completion operations must be declared separately

If the intended cognitive operation is “glue pieces and then infer a larger atomic whole,” a second operation is required. Several mathematically inequivalent completions are possible.

| Completion | Input condition | Added structure | Key warning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Top-simplex filler | all proper faces of a specified \(\Delta^n\) are present | add the declared \(n\)-simplex | provenance/filler declaration is extra data |
| Flag/clique completion | a graph/1-skeleton | add every clique as a simplex | far stronger than ordinary gluing; may add many high faces |
| Horn filling | a simplicial-set horn \(\Lambda_k^n\to X\) | choose an extension \(\Delta^n\to X\) | fillers need not exist or be unique unless extra axioms hold |
| CW attachment | map \(S^{n-1}\to X\) | attach an \(n\)-cell | output is naturally a CW complex, not necessarily a simplicial complex without triangulation |
| Semantic closure | formulas/constraints plus a closure operator | add consequences | output depends on the chosen logic/closure system |

The completion policy should never be hidden inside the word “glue.”

## 5. Other gluing/composition notions

### 5.1 Join

For complexes \(K,L\) on disjoint vertex sets,
\[
K*L=\{\sigma\cup\tau:\sigma\in K,\tau\in L\}.
\]
The join **does** introduce all mixed simplices required by the definition. If \(K=\Delta(A)\) and \(L=\Delta(B)\), then
\[
\Delta(A)*\Delta(B)=\Delta(A\sqcup B).
\]
This makes join excellent for a notion of independent combinatorial factors, but dangerously weak if one begins with a simplex: every partition of its vertices yields a join decomposition.

### 5.2 Wedge

A wedge identifies chosen basepoints. It is useful for “share exactly one distinguished concept” but typically does not model attribute composition because it adds no mixed faces.

### 5.3 Products

Products depend on category. Geometric products of realizations, categorical products of abstract complexes, and products of simplicial sets are not interchangeable. They are better suited to independent coordinate systems than to the thesis's common-face examples.

### 5.4 Nerve

Given a family \(\{C_i\}\), the nerve \(N\) has a vertex for each \(C_i\) and a simplex \(\{i_0,\ldots,i_k\}\) exactly when the total intersection \(C_{i_0}\cap\cdots\cap C_{i_k}\) is nonempty. The nerve records **assembly/intersection pattern**, not the internal contents of each concept. Under good-cover hypotheses, it recovers the union's homotopy type.

### 5.5 Sheaf gluing

A presheaf \(\mathcal F\) assigns local data to regions and restriction maps to inclusions. It is a sheaf if compatible local sections over a cover glue to a **unique** global section. For ordinary Set-valued sheaves, equality on pairwise overlaps is the required compatibility condition; no independent triple-overlap axiom is needed once the restriction maps satisfy presheaf functoriality.

### 5.6 Cosheaf aggregation

A cosheaf reverses the variance: local information maps forward into larger regions and is reconstructed by a colimit condition. This is often conceptually closer to “aggregate parts into a whole,” whereas a sheaf is closer to “test whether local descriptions are globally coherent.” The two should not be conflated.

### 5.7 Boolean/logical composition

If concept semantics are encoded by Boolean relations or functions, operations such as conjunction may be defined independently of the simplicial carrier. The thesis's formulaic reconstructions belong here. A logical conjunction that recovers \(X\land Y\land Z\) is not automatically the same operation as union of three edges in a complex.


### 5.8 Comparative contract for the candidate gluing notions

The prompt asks that each candidate operation be checked against the same seven questions. The following table fixes those contracts. “Associative” means associative up to canonical isomorphism where the construction is categorical; “recoverable” refers to recovery from the **unmarked output** unless stated otherwise.

| Construction | Inputs | Compatibility data | Output type | Unintended/new faces? | Associative / order dependence | Functorial? | Are original components intrinsically recoverable? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| common-face identification / simplicial pushout | complexes and maps \(D\to A,D\to B\) | maps must be simplicial; embeddings if literal common-face gluing is intended | simplicial complex | no completion; only images of input simplices survive, modulo identifications | binary pushouts compose through the corresponding finite colimit; parenthesization is harmless only after the diagram is fixed | yes, as a colimit construction | generally no; yes from a marked pushout diagram |
| pushout in simplicial sets | simplicial sets and simplicial maps | matching domain plus simplicial identities | simplicial set | no extra nondegenerate simplex merely from having its boundary; degeneracies are inherited categorically | canonical up to isomorphism as a colimit | yes | generally no without marked maps |
| literal union with prescribed \(\sigma\cap\tau=\rho\) | subcomplexes of an ambient complex | actual intersection must equal the declared overlap | simplicial complex | no | ordinary finite union is associative/commutative | functorial only relative to compatible ambient maps | generally no cover provenance from the union alone |
| join \(K*L\) | complexes on disjoint (or renamed-disjoint) vertices | disjoint factor supports | simplicial complex | **yes by design**: every cross-union \(\sigma\cup\tau\) is inserted | associative and commutative up to canonical isomorphism | yes | finest join factors can be canonical; coarse factors need not be unique |
| categorical/geometric product | objects in a declared category | coordinate maps; category must be fixed | product object; realization may not be simplicial without subdivision | not “faces” in the join sense; product cells/simplices depend on model | associative up to isomorphism | yes | factor recovery is a separate prime-factor problem and can fail to be unique in broad categories |
| wedge | pointed objects | chosen basepoints | pointed complex/space | no mixed faces beyond the identification | associative up to pointed isomorphism | yes for pointed maps | basepoint and wedge summands need not be intrinsic in arbitrary output |
| general colimit | a diagram of objects/morphisms | the full diagram | object of the chosen category | exactly those forced by that category's colimit, not a generic closure | diagram-independent parenthesization when computing the same colimit | yes | no in general; the diagram is extra provenance |
| CW attachment | \(X\), an \((n-1)\)-sphere and attaching map | continuous attaching map | CW complex | **yes by declaration**: a new \(n\)-cell is added | multiple attachments are order-independent only under explicit hypotheses/diagram formulations | functorial only for maps compatible with attaching data | attaching data are not normally determined by the unmarked result |
| horn filling | horn map \(\Lambda_k^n\to X\) | a chosen extension must exist | simplicial set with/through a filler | **yes by declaration**: an \(n\)-simplex filler | choice-dependent unless fillers are specified or unique | natural only in structures with coherent chosen fillers | not if several fillers exist |
| nerve | a family/cover \(\{U_i\}\) | finite-intersection incidences | index simplicial complex | simplices encode nonempty total intersections | independent of ordering of the index set up to relabeling | functorial for suitable cover maps | no; internal contents of \(U_i\) are discarded |
| flag/clique closure | graph or 1-skeleton | none beyond the graph | flag complex | **yes**, every clique becomes a simplex | deterministic/idempotent closure | yes for graph maps that induce simplicial maps | the pre-closure declaration of higher faces is lost |
| sheaf gluing | sheaf sections \(s_i\in F(U_i)\) | equality on pairwise overlaps | a global section, not a carrier simplex | not applicable to carrier faces | unique and order-independent once the cover is fixed | yes under morphisms of sheaves/sites | locals are recovered by restriction from the global section on the same cover |
| cosheaf aggregation | local cosheaf data over a cover | structure maps and the cosheaf colimit condition | global aggregate | not applicable to carrier faces | categorical colimit behavior | yes | generally not without injections/provenance; cosheaf axiom is about assembly, not factor recovery |
| Boolean/logical composition | formulas/relations/functions | shared-variable semantics and chosen connective/composition | formula/function/relation | may create semantic interaction terms, not geometric faces | depends on connective; \(\land,\lor,\oplus\) are associative, arbitrary compiler/composition need not be | syntax/semantic-map dependent | factor recovery is a Boolean/relational factorization problem, generally not unique without a prime criterion |

Two consequences are important. First, **pushout/union, completion, and join have different face-creation policies** and therefore cannot be alternate notations for one operation. Second, recoverability is usually a property of a marked diagram or a separate factorization theorem, not of colimits themselves.

## 6. Higher-order concept

No single historical use of “order” is mathematically stable: the thesis uses simplicial dimension, number of fixed attributes, p-adic depth, and logical conjunction in related ways. The modern project should use typed notions:

- **simplicial order**: \(\dim \sigma\) or \(\dim K\);
- **attribute order**: number/depth of semantic attributes;
- **assembly order**: position in a declared colimit/composition diagram;
- **logical order**: arity/complexity of the formula or relation.

The most useful neutral definition is:

> A **higher-order concept relative to a diagram** \(D\) is a structured object \(C\) equipped with a specified universal/semantic assembly map from the lower-order inputs, usually a pushout/colimit followed, if desired, by an explicitly named completion functor.

This makes “higher” relational rather than pretending that every dimension measure agrees.

## 7. Recoverability and provenance

A categorical colimit is unique up to isomorphism, but a bare output object generally does not determine the input diagram that produced it. Therefore define two variants:

**Unmarked gluing:** return only \(C=A\cup_D B\).

**Marked gluing:** return \((C;\iota_A,\iota_B,\iota_D)\), retaining the distinguished images of the pieces and overlap.

Marked gluing is the appropriate notion if “disentanglement” is supposed to recover the historical constituents. Unmarked gluing is appropriate only when decomposition is to be inferred intrinsically by a canonical factorization theorem.

## 8. Proposed category for the next theorem phase

A minimal research category \(\mathbf{SConcept}\) can have objects
\[
(K,\lambda,R)
\]
where \(K\) is a finite complex, \(\lambda\) labels vertices/faces, and \(R\) is a finite relation on a declared attribute set (or, in the CM specialization, a Boolean truth tensor). Morphisms should preserve faces and labels and map satisfying assignments consistently.

A richer variant replaces \(R\) by a presheaf/sheaf \(\mathcal F\) on the face poset. The project should prove results first for one precise category rather than allowing all semantic layers simultaneously.

## 9. Priority conclusion

All basic constructions in this document are standard mathematics. In particular, category-theoretic conceptual blending has already been explicitly modeled via colimits/pushouts/amalgams, and modern work continues that program. The project contribution cannot be “concepts can be glued by pushouts.” Its plausible contribution is a **carefully delimited structured concept calculus that compares several inequivalent gluing and factorization notions and proves when they agree**.

# Gluing Concepts — Master Mathematical Audit

**Working title:** *Gluing Concepts: Composition, Reconstruction, and Clean Decomposition in Simplicial Mental Spaces*  
**Historical source:** Brian Droncheff, *On the Ultrametric Unconscious, Quantum Consciousness, and Mental Spaces* (2015)  
**Audit date:** 28 September 2026  
**Status:** research audit and finite-computation package; not a publication or novelty claim.

---

## 1. Executive determination

The historical thesis contains a real and recoverable mathematical research seed, but it combines several operations that must be separated before the program becomes rigorous:

1. **simplicial gluing:** assemble subcomplexes along specified overlaps;
2. **completion/filling:** add a higher-dimensional simplex/cell not present in the pieces;
3. **local-to-global semantic gluing:** reconstruct globally coherent data from compatible restrictions;
4. **factorization/separability:** decompose a structured whole into genuinely independent factors.

The central correction is that these operations are **not equivalent**. In particular, the union of all faces of a simplex is generally its boundary, not the filled simplex, and decomposition into faces is not decomposition into independent factors.

### Recommended ontology

Adopt the two-level model requested in option 3:

- an **atomic concept** is a finite labelled simplex;
- a **conceptual/mental structure** is a finite simplicial complex assembled from atomic concepts;
- any nontrivial claim about independence, semantics, or recoverability uses a **structured concept**
  \[
  \mathcal C=(K,\lambda,\mathcal S),
  \]
  where \(K\) is the carrier complex, \(\lambda\) is label/provenance data, and \(\mathcal S\) is a declared semantic layer such as a finite relation, Boolean/CM object, or sheaf.

This preserves both historical uses of “concept” without silently identifying a simplex with an arbitrary connected complex.

### End-state assessment

\[
\boxed{\textbf{Outcome 4 — Requires additional structure}}
\]

Bare simplices make join decomposition too permissive: every vertex partition of a simplex gives a join factorization. Ordinary simplicial gluing is standard and non-completing. The project becomes mathematically substantive only after labels, logical constraints, semantic relations, provenance, sheaf data, or CM structure are added.

The most promising next result is not another gluing construction. It is the **succinct structured factorization problem**: compute the finest partition across which both a compact simplicial carrier and an intensionally represented Boolean/CM semantic layer factor, without expanding the full truth table.

---

## 2. Historical recovery: what the thesis actually says

The thesis is treated here as a fixed historical source, not as mathematical authority. The following source map is also supplied machine-readably in `data/thesis_source_map.csv`.

| Thesis location | Topic | Classification | Historical content | Modern assessment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PDF pp. 26–29 | simplices, complexes, chains | precise setup | Introduces simplicial/chain language and foreshadows concepts as complexes. | Retain standard definitions only; cycles are not automatically concepts/symmetries. |
| p. 50 | \(X\land Y\) as higher-order concept | historical intuition | Calls a conjunction a higher-order concept and suggests distinguishing constituents by measurement. | Semantic composition seed; not yet simplicial gluing. |
| p. 52 | definition of concept | precise definition + unsupported claims | Defines a concept as a connected simplicial complex with pairwise edge connectivity, then makes topological claims. | Best modernized as an atomic-simplex/complex distinction, with topology stated separately. |
| pp. 54–55 | concept order / p-adic hierarchy | intuition + examples | Order tracks fixed attributes / p-adic depth. | Keep distinct from simplicial dimension. |
| pp. 56–58 | Matte-Blanco unfolding / \(\partial\) | intuition + thesis definition | Defines a logical “unfolding” that omits a vertex, negates it, and disjoins terms. | This is **not** the standard simplicial boundary. |
| pp. 59–60 | triangle unfolding; green-box | worked examples | Decomposes logical simplices into differentiated lower-order pieces. | Separate logical transformation from geometric face exposure. |
| p. 61 | explicit gluing motivation | historical intuition | After unfolding, asks to build lower-dimensional expressions back up by “gluing” or “integrating.” | This is the core recoverability question. |
| pp. 62–63 | triangle reconstruction; tetrahedron; “integrator” | worked examples + unsupported claim/open question | Conjoins side formulas to recover \(X\land Y\land Z\); says four triangular faces build a tetrahedron and asks for an integrator, mentioning CW complexes. | Boolean reconstruction is distinct from simplicial union; four faces give \(\partial\Delta^3\), so a filler is extra data. |
| p. 66 | shared p-adic attributes | intuition | Uses intersections to encode common attributes. | Natural overlap object, but representation-specific padding must not be universalized. |
| pp. 74–80 | ProLT, presheaves, restrictions | definitions + proposed extension | Introduces presheaf-like restrictions and aims to build larger complexes by gluing smaller concepts. | Genuine sheaf gluing requires existence and uniqueness, not just restrictions. |
| p. 82 | relative topology and compatible sections | historical intuition + close modern analogue | Proposes gluing compatible sections into sheaves or higher-order concepts. | Closest sound analogue is ordinary sheaf descent. |
| pp. 86–87 | overlapping concepts; “pink flower” | worked example + unsupported recoverability | Unfolds overlapping concepts and says partition pieces can be glued back. | Requires a specified semantic gluing map and retained provenance. |
| pp. 88–91 | logical triangles/squares | worked diagrams + possible analogue | “Glues” logical triangles sharing operators into exact squares; some pairs fail. | Treat as algebraic/diagrammatic compatibility, not automatically as a simplicial pushout. |

### Historical conclusion

There are **two distinct gluing seeds** in the thesis:

- a geometric/logical **face-reconstruction** seed (triangle/tetrahedron/integrator);
- a semantic **compatible-sections** seed (presheaf/sheaf/local-to-global).

They should be developed separately and compared only after each is formalized.

---

## 3. What should “gluing” mean?

No single operation covers all intended cases. The default should be the least committal construction.

### 3.1 Default: pushout along a specified common subcomplex

Given embeddings
\[
D\hookrightarrow A,\qquad D\hookrightarrow B,
\]
define gluing as the pushout \(A\cup_D B\). When these are literal subcomplex inclusions, it is the ordinary simplicial union with the overlap identified.

**Key property:** it is **non-completing**. A new simplex does not appear merely because all its vertices are present in the pushout.

This is the mathematically clean model of “identify exactly the shared part.” It is associative up to the usual canonical isomorphism when organized as a colimit diagram, functorial in the diagram, and recoverable only if the input embeddings/provenance are retained.

### 3.2 Operations that must remain distinct

| Operation | Appropriate use | Does it add mixed/higher simplices? | Recoverability |
|---|---|---:|---|
| union/pushout along inclusion | exact common-face assembly | no | only with marked subobjects or intrinsic factor theorem |
| join | free combination of disjoint structural factors | yes, all cross-faces | canonical finest factors exist, but simplex case trivializes |
| wedge | share one basepoint | no mixed faces | basepoint-dependent |
| product | coordinate/product structure | category-dependent | can represent independent coordinates |
| colimit | general diagrammatic assembly | depends on category | diagram not determined by bare colimit |
| CW attachment | add a cell along boundary map | yes, declared cell | attachment map is essential data |
| horn filling | simplicial-set completion | adds chosen filler | existence/uniqueness need extra axioms |
| flag/clique completion | infer simplices from 1-skeleton cliques | potentially many | destroys information about which higher faces were explicit |
| nerve | record intersection pattern of pieces | creates an index complex | loses internal content of pieces |
| sheaf gluing | coherent local semantic data | produces global section, not carrier simplex | unique if sheaf axiom holds |
| cosheaf aggregation | aggregate local contributions | colimit-like | depends on cosheaf structure |
| Boolean conjunction / semantic composition | combine constraints/formulas | semantic, not automatically geometric | factorability depends on logic |

### 3.3 When does ordinary gluing produce one larger simplex?

For two simplices \(\Delta(S),\Delta(T)\), their ordinary union is a simplex iff one is contained in the other. If neither contains the other, some edge between a vertex unique to each side is missing. Therefore a higher simplex almost never arises from nontrivial ordinary gluing alone.

If “higher-order concept” is intended to mean a new filled simplex, the theory requires a **separate completion/filler operator**.

---

## 4. Higher-order concepts

The thesis uses “order” in several incompatible senses. The modern theory should type them explicitly:

- **simplicial order:** dimension;
- **attribute order:** number/depth of constrained semantic attributes;
- **assembly order:** position in a composition/colimit diagram;
- **logical order:** formula arity/complexity;
- **global-section order:** a global semantic state determined by a cover.

The most fertile formal definition is relational:

> A higher-order concept relative to a diagram is a structured object equipped with a declared assembly map from lower-order inputs, typically a colimit/pushout followed, when desired, by an explicitly named completion or semantic closure.

This avoids pretending these order notions are equivalent.

---

## 5. Clean gluing criteria

### 5.1 Simplicial carrier

A clean common-face gluing diagram should state:

1. the intended overlaps \(C_i\cap C_j\);
2. embeddings are injective away from the declared identifications;
3. the colimit lies in the intended category;
4. no completion is silently applied;
5. constituent images remain marked if historical recovery matters.

For inclusions of subcomplexes, these are straightforward and pairwise/higher intersections are inherited from the actual subobjects.

### 5.2 Semantic labels

Labels/attribute assignments must agree on identified vertices/faces. If the semantic layer is a presheaf/sheaf, restrictions must be functorial.

### 5.3 Sheaf compatibility

For a genuine Set-valued sheaf \(\mathcal F\) and cover \(U=\bigcup_iU_i\), the exact condition is
\[
s_i|_{U_i\cap U_j}=s_j|_{U_i\cap U_j}\quad\forall i,j.
\]
Then there exists a **unique** \(s\in\mathcal F(U)\) restricting to all \(s_i\). Pairwise agreement is sufficient in ordinary Set-valued sheaf theory; separate triple-overlap coherence is not an additional axiom.

A presheaf can fail this property; Example D below gives an exact failure.

---

## 6. Decomposition and “disentanglement”

The project should use **factorization/separability** as the neutral vocabulary.

Three problems must be separated:

1. **face decomposition:** expose lower-dimensional faces;
2. **assembly decomposition:** recover a chosen cover/pushout diagram;
3. **independent-factor decomposition:** partition variables/vertices into blocks with no mixed interaction according to a declared criterion.

Only the third is strong disentanglement.

### 6.1 Structural independence by join

For \(V=A\sqcup B\), define
\[
K\text{ structurally factors across }A|B
\iff
K=K|_A*K|_B.
\]
This says every allowed face on one side can combine freely with every allowed face on the other.

The exact criterion is that no minimal nonface crosses the partition. Connected components of the minimal-nonface hypergraph yield the canonical finest join factors.

### 6.2 Why a simplex is too weak

A simplex has no minimal nonfaces, so for every partition
\[
\Delta(V)=*_{B\in\Pi}\Delta(B).
\]
Thus a bare simplex treats **every partition** as structurally independent. This is the central reason the project ends in Outcome 4 rather than a simplex-only theory.

### 6.3 Semantic independence by finite relation

For admissible assignments \(R\) across attribute blocks, define independence by Cartesian product factorization. The extensional finite relation has a canonical prime factorization in established database theory.

### 6.4 CM/Boolean separability

The supplied current CM/LM manuscript proves the fixed-bipartition theorem
\[
f(a,b)=g(a)\land h(b)
\iff
\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F_2}[f]_{A|B}\le1,
\]
and identifies ordinary \(\mathbb F_2\)-rank with the minimum XOR sum of conjunctive factors. This is immediately useful as a semantic interaction measure, but broad Boolean decomposition is classical, so priority claims must remain narrow.

### 6.5 Cross-layer criterion

A robust clean decomposition should require **the same partition** to factor both the simplicial carrier and the semantic layer. This prevents a simplex's trivial structural factorability from deciding the semantics.

For an extensional finite relation, if \(\Pi_K\) is the finest structural partition and \(\Pi_R\) the prime semantic partition, the finest simultaneous partition is their **least common coarsening**. This is proved in `DECOMPOSITION_AND_SEPARABILITY.md`.

The package also contains a four-attribute example where both layers factor nontrivially but across crossing partitions, so the structured object has no nontrivial simultaneous factorization.

---

## 7. Gluing versus unfolding

The thesis's historical \(\partial\) should not be reused as the standard chain boundary. Use separate notation:

- \(\partial_{\mathrm{ch}}\): homological boundary;
- \(U\): unfolding/restriction;
- \(G\): gluing/colimit;
- \(F\): filler/completion.

### 7.1 Plain gluing is not an inverse

For a tetrahedron, deleting the top simplex exposes its four triangular faces. Re-union of those faces gives only the boundary:
\[
G(U(\Delta^3))=\partial\Delta^3\neq\Delta^3.
\]

### 7.2 A partial inverse is possible with provenance

If an unfolded object is **marked** as “the boundary of this labelled simplex,” a filler can reinsert the top simplex. That gives a restricted partial inverse on a declared subcategory, not an intrinsic inverse on bare complexes.

### 7.3 Sheaf restriction/gluing is the cleanest inverse paradigm

If “unfolding” is reinterpreted as restriction of a global semantic section to a cover, then the sheaf axiom reconstructs the unique global section from its compatible restrictions. That is the strongest rigorous form of the thesis's inverse intuition presently available.

It still does **not** imply that the global section factors into independent constituents.

---

## 8. Chain-level gluing

For \(K=A\cup B\) and \(D=A\cap B\):
\[
0\to C_\bullet(D)
\to C_\bullet(A)\oplus C_\bullet(B)
\to C_\bullet(K)\to0
\]
with maps \(x\mapsto(x,-x)\) and \((a,b)\mapsto a+b\). This yields Mayer–Vietoris.

The exact sequence gives a rigorous bridge between overlap and global topology. Connecting homomorphisms can expose cycles created by the gluing pattern. Relative homology and mapping cones can measure what one piece adds beyond the overlap.

However, homology is not a complete independence detector. The package gives a contractible but join-irreducible four-vertex complex.

Likewise, degreewise vector-space splitting over a field is noncanonical and therefore too weak to count as conceptual independence.

---

## 9. Nerve analysis

For a cover \(\{C_i\}\), the nerve has:

- one vertex per constituent concept;
- an edge for nonempty pairwise overlap;
- a \(k\)-simplex for a nonempty \((k+1)\)-fold intersection.

It is an excellent **assembly/intersection invariant**. Under a good-cover hypothesis, it recovers the union's homotopy type.

It is not a full reconstruction of the internal concepts: two covers with the same nerve can have very different piece contents. The current ProLT manuscript correctly treats its relation nerve as presentation-dependent; that caution should carry over here.

---

## 10. Sheaf/cosheaf reconstruction

The thesis's late presheaf language is more mathematically promising for reconstruction than its tetrahedral picture.

### Sheaf role

A sheaf answers:

> Can locally specified concept states coexist as one unique global state?

This is a **coherence** question.

### Cosheaf role

A cosheaf is better suited to:

> Can local contributions be aggregated into a global object by a colimit-type rule?

This is an **aggregation** question.

### Independence is a third question

Neither coherence nor aggregation implies factorization. A complete structured theory can therefore use:

- simplicial carrier: overlap/assembly geometry;
- sheaf: semantic consistency;
- cosheaf: aggregation;
- relation/Boolean/CM layer: factorization and interaction.

This four-way separation is preferable to asking one structure to do all jobs.

---

## 11. Exact Examples A–G

All simplicial computations are reproduced by `code/gluing_audit.py`; exact records are in `data/finite_examples.json/.csv` and `data/diagnostics.json`.

### Example A — two concepts glued along a vertex

Facets: \(ab,bc\).  
Result: a path with \(f=(3,2)\), \(\beta=(1,0)\).  
Recoverability: exact if the two embedded input edges are marked; otherwise the historical cover is provenance.

### Example B — two filled triangles glued along an edge

Facets: \(abc,bcd\), overlap \(bc\).  
Result: a triangulated disk with \(f=(4,5,2)\), \(\beta=(1,0,0)\).  
Mayer–Vietoris is homologically trivial because all pieces and the union are contractible, although the chain-level identification is nontrivial.

### Example C — tetrahedron from triangular faces

Four-face union:
\[
\partial\Delta^3,
\qquad
f=(4,6,4),
\qquad
\beta=(1,0,1).
\]
Filled tetrahedron:
\[
\Delta^3,
\qquad
f=(4,6,4,1),
\qquad
\beta=(1,0,0,0).
\]
All four faces are insufficient under plain union. Three faces form a horn-like disk; under a declared horn-filling condition they may admit a filler. Under flag completion, the \(K_4\) 1-skeleton alone already forces the tetrahedron.

### Example D — compatible local data with no global gluing

Discrete \(X=\{p,q\}\); presheaf \(P(W)=\mathbb Z\) on nonempty opens and \(P(\varnothing)=\{*\}\). Local sections 0 and 1 agree vacuously on the empty overlap but no global integer restricts by identity to both.

This is possible for a presheaf; it is excluded by the sheaf axiom.

### Example E — clean factorization

Four-cycle with minimal nonfaces \(a_0a_1\) and \(b_0b_1\).  
It is exactly
\[
K|_{\{a_0,a_1\}}*K|_{\{b_0,b_1\}},
\]
with \(\beta=(1,1)\).

### Example F — irreducible interaction

On the same four vertices, minimal nonfaces \(a_0a_1,a_1b_0,b_0b_1\) connect the interaction hypergraph. The resulting path is contractible but has no nontrivial join factorization.

### Example G — smallest nonunique coarse join decomposition

The filled triangle has three distinct unordered binary join decompositions, but one unique finest decomposition into singleton vertices. This distinguishes coarse nonuniqueness from canonical prime decomposition.

---

## 12. Exhaustive finite computation and speedups

The program enumerated all labeled simplicial complexes **using all vertices** through \(n=5\):

| vertices | complexes | join-indecomposable | nontrivially join-decomposable | unordered partition checks | failures |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 2 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 0 |
| 3 | 9 | 5 | 4 | 27 | 0 |
| 4 | 114 | 84 | 30 | 798 | 0 |
| 5 | 6,894 | 6,348 | 546 | 103,410 | 0 |

Totals: **7,020 complexes**, **104,237 bipartition checks**, zero disagreements with the minimal-nonface criterion, and zero failures of finest-factor reconstruction.

### Speedups before brute force

1. **Do not enumerate partitions to find the finest structural factors.** Compute minimal nonfaces, connect co-occurring vertices, and take components.
2. **Flag complexes:** join decomposition reduces to connected components of the complement graph.
3. **Use isomorphism classes/canonical generation** for larger finite classification rather than labeled Dedekind enumeration.
4. **Semantic relation:** use relational prime-factorization algorithms rather than scanning every attribute partition.
5. **Fixed CM cut:** use ordinary \(\mathbb F_2\) rank directly.
6. **Cross-layer decomposition:** compute each prime partition first, then take their least common coarsening instead of testing every common partition.

The computational campaign validates the formal criteria; it does not itself establish novelty.

---

## 13. Literature/priority conclusion through 2026

The full source-by-source audit is in `LITERATURE_PRIORITY_MAP.md` and `data/literature_priority_map.csv`.

The closest priority barriers are:

- conceptual blending already modeled categorically by colimits/pushouts/amalgams;
- sheafification already proposed as a universal construction for semantic compositionality;
- unique finest join decompositions already appear in current simplicial/set-family literature;
- Boolean function decomposition is classical;
- relational prime product factorization has polynomial algorithms;
- Formal Concept Analysis has explicit mature theories of factors, concept-lattice decompositions, and recent independent-subcontext work.

Therefore the project should **not** claim novelty for pushout gluing, sheaf gluing, join factorization, Boolean decomposition, or “concept decomposition” broadly.

What survives is a potentially valuable synthesis: **require structural, semantic, and eventually local-to-global layers to agree on the same decomposition**, and study the algorithmics/obstructions of that agreement.

---

## 14. Answers to the project's 15 required questions

1. **Cleanest definition of a simplicial concept?**  
   Atomic labelled simplex + concept complex + optional semantic layer. This resolves the thesis's simplex/complex ambiguity without deleting either use.

2. **What does it mean to glue concepts?**  
   By default, a pushout/colimit along explicitly declared overlap maps. Completion is a second operation.

3. **What compatibility is necessary/sufficient?**  
   For the carrier: well-typed overlap maps/identifications. For labels: equality/compatibility on identified data. For sheaves: matching sections on pairwise overlaps, with the sheaf axiom supplying unique gluing.

4. **When does gluing produce a higher-order simplex?**  
   Plain union of two simplices only when one contains the other. Nontrivial higher simplices require a completion rule such as a declared filler, flag closure, or horn filler.

5. **When can constituents be recovered?**  
   Always from a **marked** gluing diagram; generally not from the bare colimit. Intrinsic recovery requires a canonical factorization theorem.

6. **Correct notion of independent concepts?**  
   No unqualified notion. Use structural join independence, semantic Cartesian independence, CM fixed-cut rank separability, or probabilistic independence only in their proper domains.

7. **When is a higher concept separable/factorizable?**  
   When the declared layer factors across a partition; for robust structured separability, require the same partition across carrier and semantics.

8. **When is it irreducible?**  
   When its canonical finest admissible partition is one block. The minimal-nonface hypergraph detects this for structural join factorization.

9. **Is decomposition unique/canonical?**  
   Coarse decompositions need not be unique. The finest join decomposition and prime relational product decomposition are canonical in their respective settings. Their finest simultaneous partition is the least common coarsening.

10. **Is unfolding inverse to gluing?**  
    Not on bare complexes. A partial inverse is possible with declared filler/provenance; sheaf restriction/gluing gives a genuine local-to-global inverse statement at the section level.

11. **Faces versus independent factors?**  
    Fundamentally different. Boundary faces overlap; independent factors require free recombination/product structure.

12. **Do homology/Mayer–Vietoris/cohomology detect interaction?**  
    They can detect topological obstruction/attachment, but not all factorization. Contractible irreducible examples show homology is incomplete for independence.

13. **Can Correspondence Matrices help?**  
    Yes. The current CM flattening theorem gives an exact fixed-cut rank criterion for conjunctive/XOR separability. Its advantage should be studied algorithmically rather than assumed.

14. **Is there a theorem-level contribution beyond standard gluing?**  
    Not yet established as novel. The cross-layer least-common-coarsening theorem is useful but elementary once prime factors are known. The promising theorem-level work is succinct structured factorization and possibly sheaf/CM interaction.

15. **Connection to the broader Mental Space program?**  
    Strong as a mathematical architecture: simplicial carrier for incidence, ultrametric/other geometry for similarity, sheaf/cosheaf for local-global information, and Boolean/CM constraints for factorization. Psychological interpretation should remain a modeling hypothesis until independently justified.

---

## 15. The strongest theorem / finite classification problem to attack next

### Succinct Structured Factorization

**Input:**

- a finite simplicial complex \(K\) in a compact representation (facets, minimal nonfaces, flag graph, etc.);
- a Boolean semantic object \(f\) over the same attributes, represented intensionally by CNF/DNF/circuit/ANF or CM/LM data.

**Goal:** output the unique finest partition \(\Pi\) on which **both** layers factor, or certify that the one-block partition is the only simultaneous factorization, **without enumerating the full truth relation**.

The extensional relation case is already reduced to:

1. canonical simplicial join partition;
2. prime relational product partition;
3. least common coarsening.

The real mathematical problem is the succinct semantic case. The next paper-worthy result should establish either:

- a polynomial/FPT algorithm for a substantial class with a canonical invariant, or
- hardness for the general case together with a sharp tractable frontier.

This is more promising than extending brute-force counts to six vertices without a conjecture.

---

## 16. Final project classification

### Outcome 4 — Requires additional structure

The unification does **not** fail, but it must be conditional:

\[
\boxed{
\text{carrier gluing}
+\text{explicit completion}
+\text{semantic coherence}
+\text{factorization structure}
}
\]

is a coherent program.

What should be abandoned is the stronger historical identification

\[
\text{gluing faces}
=\text{recovering a filled simplex}
=\text{unfolding inverse}
=\text{independent-factor decomposition}.
\]

Those equalities are false in general. Once they are separated, the research direction becomes substantially cleaner and, in the structured/succinct factorization problem, potentially mathematically productive.

---

## 17. Package map

Required deliverables:

- `GLUING_CONCEPTS_MASTER_AUDIT.md` — this document.
- `FORMAL_GLUING_DEFINITIONS.md` — precise ontology and gluing operations.
- `DECOMPOSITION_AND_SEPARABILITY.md` — structural/semantic/CM factorization and simultaneous partition theorem.
- `GLUING_VS_UNFOLDING.md` — why gluing, filling, unfolding, and factorization differ.
- `CHAIN_LEVEL_GLUING.md` — exact chain sequence, Mayer–Vietoris, relative homology, mapping-cone interpretation.
- `SHEAF_LOCAL_TO_GLOBAL_ANALYSIS.md` — matching families, presheaf counterexample, sheaf/cosheaf roles.
- `FINITE_EXAMPLES.md` — exact A–G examples and finite enumeration.
- `LITERATURE_PRIORITY_MAP.md` — structure-based literature/priority audit through 2026.
- `THEOREMS_COUNTEREXAMPLES_OPEN_PROBLEMS.md` — consolidated theorem/counterexample/open-problem ledger.
- `data/research_ledger.csv` — concise requested ledger.
- `data/thesis_source_map.csv` — historical source map.
- `data/*.json/.csv` — exact machine-readable computation outputs.
- `code/gluing_audit.py` — reproducible standard-library computation.
